questions.stem: A 32-year-old man develops crampy abdominal pain and watery diarrhea two days after eating undercooked food at a picnic. Stool culture grows a bacterial pathogen. Which of the following is the most likely portal of entry for this organism?

explanation.summary: Most gastrointestinal pathogens enter through ingestion of food or water contaminated with fecal matter.
explanation.whyCorrect: The GI tract is a common portal of entry when its defenses (gastric acid, peristalsis, IgA, and normal microbiota) are overcome. Food or water contaminated by feces delivers the organism, and abdominal pain with diarrhea points to a gut infection acquired by the fecal-oral route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The urethra is the entry point for urinary tract, not gastrointestinal, pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Broken skin is a portal for wound and catheter-associated infections, not enteric disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhalation delivers respiratory pathogens to the airways, not organisms causing diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retrograde neuronal transport is how certain viruses reach the CNS, not how gut bacteria are acquired.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A physiologist studies how the upper airway resists infection. She observes that inhaled particles are trapped in a sticky mucus layer and swept by hair-like projections toward the throat, where they are cleared. Which of the following defense mechanisms is being described?

explanation.summary: The respiratory tract relies on mucociliary clearance to trap and remove inhaled microbes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucus traps large particles while cilia beat them toward the back of the throat for clearance; only small particles reach the alveoli, where immune cells phagocytose them. This trapping-and-sweeping description defines mucociliary clearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antimicrobial fatty acids are a defense of the skin surface, not the airway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Urinary flushing is a urogenital defense that clears organisms from the urethra.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric acidity is a gastrointestinal defense that kills ingested organisms in the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peristalsis is the wave-like movement of the GI tract that prevents microbial overgrowth.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman hospitalized for pneumonia is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and then develops profuse watery diarrhea. Colonoscopy reveals adherent yellow-white plaques on the colonic mucosa, and toxin testing is positive. Which of the following best explains her increased susceptibility to this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breakdown of the keratinized epidermal barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disruption of the normal gut microbiota

explanation.summary: Antibiotics disrupt the protective gut microbiota, allowing C. difficile overgrowth and pseudomembranous colitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The normal gut microbiota competes with arriving organisms and limits their colonization. Antibiotics kill this resident flora, letting C. difficile proliferate and release toxins A and B, which produce the inflammatory pseudomembrane seen on the mucosa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The epidermal barrier guards the skin, not the gut lumen where this infection occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucociliary clearance is a respiratory defense, unrelated to colonic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric acid protects against ingested organisms but is not the defense lost with antibiotic use.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine flow is a urogenital defense and has no role in colonic colonization.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A neonate develops purulent conjunctivitis three days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The mother had an untreated sexually transmitted infection. Which of the following best describes how the pathogen was transmitted to the infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exposure during passage through the birth canal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding from a distant maternal focus

explanation.summary: Some pathogens are transmitted vertically as the infant passes through the birth canal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exposure during passage through the birth canal transmits organisms such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, leading to neonatal conjunctivitis. The timing right after vaginal delivery and the maternal genital infection point to this route.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematogenous seeding describes spread within a host's bloodstream, not mother-to-infant transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breast milk transmits certain viruses (e.g., CMV, HIV, HBV) postnatally, not this early bacterial conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory droplet inhalation is a person-to-person route unrelated to this genital pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplacental spread in utero characterizes TORCH agents and would cause congenital disease present at birth, not acquired during delivery.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man who injects drugs intravenously presents with fever and a new heart murmur. Echocardiography shows friable vegetations on a heart valve, and blood cultures are positive. Which of the following best explains how the organism reached the heart valve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct extension from an adjacent lung abscess

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis results from bloodborne spread of bacteria to the endocardium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravenous drug use introduces skin flora directly into the bloodstream, producing septicemia that seeds the endocardium. This hematogenous dissemination allows bacteria to form friable valvular vegetations, the hallmark of infective endocarditis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no adjacent lung abscess described, and endocarditis is not typically produced by direct extension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fecal-oral ingestion is a portal for enteric infection, not for valve seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aspiration deposits organisms in the airway, not on the endocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retrograde axonal transport carries certain viruses to the CNS, not bacteria to heart valves.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is bitten on the leg by a raccoon. Weeks later he develops difficulty swallowing, agitation, and a fatal encephalitis. By which of the following mechanisms did the causative virus most likely reach the central nervous system?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fecal-oral spread to the gastrointestinal tract

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lymphatic drainage to regional lymph nodes

explanation.summary: Some viruses travel to the CNS by retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves.
explanation.whyCorrect: Certain viruses, including rabies, spread along nerves by retrograde axonal transport, moving from the bite site backward toward the central nervous system. The animal bite followed by fatal encephalitis is the classic presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The virus is inoculated through the bite wound, not by extension across intact skin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fecal-oral spread delivers enteric pathogens to the gut, not neurotropic viruses to the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematogenous spread uses the bloodstream and is not the route rabies takes to the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphatic drainage carries organisms to lymph nodes, not directly along nerves to the CNS.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic cough and night sweats undergoes lung biopsy, which shows aggregates of epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells surrounding a central zone of caseous necrosis. Which of the following histologic patterns of reaction does this represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate without granulomas

explanation.summary: Epithelioid macrophages and giant cells around caseous necrosis define granulomatous inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatous inflammation features aggregates of activated (epithelioid) macrophages, often with giant cells; central caseating necrosis is characteristic of tuberculosis. The clinical picture of chronic cough and night sweats supports a mycobacterial granuloma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate lacks the organized epithelioid macrophages and giant cells that define a granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bland scarring is end-stage fibrosis and does not include active giant cells or caseous necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytopathic-cytoproliferative reactions are caused by viruses and show inclusion bodies, not caseating granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppurative inflammation is dominated by neutrophils and pus, not epithelioid macrophages and giant cells.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with fever has a chest CT showing multiple lung lesions filled with pus. Biopsy of one lesion reveals a localized collection of neutrophils and necrotic debris consistent with an abscess. Which of the following types of organism most commonly produces this pattern of reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inert foreign material such as talc

explanation.summary: Suppurative inflammation with abscess formation is most commonly caused by pyogenic bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Suppurative (purulent) inflammation is dominated by neutrophil infiltration, and pus is a collection of living and dying neutrophils and necrotic cells. Pyogenic bacteria are the classic cause, and an abscess is a localized collection of this pus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inert foreign material triggers granulomatous, not suppurative, inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Viruses typically produce a cytopathic-cytoproliferative reaction, not neutrophil-rich abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycobacteria produce granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis rather than pus-filled abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spirochetes such as T. pallidum characteristically elicit a mononuclear lymphocytic infiltrate.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: An immunosuppressed patient undergoes tissue biopsy that shows enlarged cells containing intranuclear inclusion bodies, with no neutrophils or granulomas present. This cytopathic pattern is most characteristic of infection by which of the following classes of pathogen?

explanation.summary: Inclusion bodies and cytopathic change without pus or granulomas point to a viral infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cytopathic-cytoproliferative pattern is produced by viruses, which cause changes such as inclusion bodies and cell lysis; CMV is a classic example in immunosuppressed patients. The absence of neutrophils and granulomas argues against bacterial or mycobacterial causes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Foreign material provokes a granulomatous foreign-body reaction, not cytopathic viral change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mycobacteria elicit granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid macrophages, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyogenic bacteria produce neutrophil-rich suppurative inflammation, not intranuclear inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spirochetes cause a lymphocytic mononuclear infiltrate rather than viral inclusion bodies.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A patient with a gram-negative bloodstream infection becomes hypotensive with signs of shock. The responsible molecule is a component of the bacterial outer membrane whose lipid portion is detected by macrophages, triggering a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Which of the following is this molecule?

explanation.summary: Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) is the gram-negative outer-membrane molecule that drives septic shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: LPS is an outer-membrane component of gram-negative bacteria whose Lipid A portion is detected by immune cells such as macrophages. This triggers pro-inflammatory and complement activation, and cytokine-induced hypotension can progress to shock.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphtheria toxin is a secreted A-B exotoxin of a gram-positive rod, not an outer-membrane lipid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococcal enterotoxin is a preformed superantigen causing food poisoning, not a gram-negative outer-membrane component.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Exfoliative toxin is a Staphylococcus aureus protein that cleaves skin desmosomes, not an endotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxic shock syndrome toxin is a secreted superantigen protein, not a structural gram-negative membrane molecule.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A child from an unvaccinated community develops a thick gray pseudomembrane over the pharynx and subsequently myocarditis. The responsible exotoxin is an A-B toxin. Which of the following best describes how its active subunit causes cell death?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insertion of Lipid A to disrupt the membrane

explanation.summary: Diphtheria toxin is an A-B toxin whose A subunit inhibits protein synthesis, causing cell death.
explanation.whyCorrect: In diphtheria, the B subunit binds and delivers the toxin into the host cell by endocytosis, and the A subunit then inhibits protein synthesis, leading to cell death. The toxin can enter the bloodstream and damage tissues such as myocardial cells, producing myocarditis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cleavage of desmoglein-1 is the mechanism of the staphylococcal exfoliative toxin, not diphtheria toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Degradation of secretory IgA is not the mechanism of diphtheria-toxin-mediated cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipid A membrane effects belong to gram-negative endotoxin, not to this gram-positive exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nonspecific massive cytokine release describes superantigens, not the diphtheria A-B toxin.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child develops widespread superficial blistering and peeling of the skin. The causative Staphylococcus aureus toxin cleaves desmoglein-1, a protein that anchors keratinocytes together. Which of the following conditions results?

explanation.summary: Exfoliative toxin cleaving desmoglein-1 produces staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exfoliative A and B toxins from S. aureus cleave desmoglein-1, a desmosomal protein, causing detachment of keratinocytes. The result is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, characterized by blistering and exfoliation that primarily affects pediatric patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphtheritic myocarditis results from diphtheria toxin inhibiting protein synthesis, not from cleaving skin proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endotoxic shock is driven by gram-negative LPS, not by a staphylococcal skin toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pseudomembranous colitis is a C. difficile toxin-mediated colonic disease, unrelated to desmoglein-1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by a superantigen and produces hypotension, not desmoglein-mediated skin peeling.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man receiving chemotherapy develops a lung infection. Culture grows an organism described as a eukaryote that possesses both a nucleus and a cell wall. To which of the following major groups of human pathogens does this organism belong?

explanation.summary: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that have both a nucleus and a cell wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus and a cell wall; Aspergillus fumigatus is the classic example and a frequent lung pathogen in immunosuppressed patients. The combination of a nucleus (eukaryote) and a cell wall distinguishes fungi from the other major pathogen groups.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacteria are prokaryotes: simple, independently living organisms with a cell wall but no nucleus or organelles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parasites are eukaryotes that depend on another host organism for survival (tapeworms, amoebas); they are not defined by a cell wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spirochetes are a type of bacterium, and therefore prokaryotic without a nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viruses are strictly intracellular pathogens that replicate using host cell machinery and lack both a nucleus and a cell wall.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man sustains deep burns over 30% of his body surface and within days develops a bacterial infection of the burned areas. Loss of which of the following skin defenses best explains his susceptibility?

explanation.summary: The skin's keratinizing squamous epithelium is its principal protective barrier, and mechanical injury such as burns breaches it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The skin defends against microbes with a protective barrier of keratinizing squamous epithelium, antimicrobial fatty acids, and antimicrobial peptides (defensins). Because this barrier is so effective, most skin infections begin with mechanical injury such as wounds, burns, cuts, bites, needle sticks, or intravenous catheters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urine flow protects the urogenital tract by washing away organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric acid is a gastrointestinal defense against ingested organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucociliary transport protects the respiratory tract, not the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA antibodies are a gastrointestinal-tract defense, not a component of the skin barrier.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman develops fever, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. Colonoscopy shows mucosal ulceration with inflammation and hemorrhage, and biopsies show organisms within the damaged mucosa. Which of the following best describes how this pathogen produces her symptoms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disruption of the normal gut microbiota

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of ciliary activity in the respiratory mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Production of a preformed toxin in food

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of a superantigen into the circulation

explanation.summary: Some GI pathogens invade the mucosa directly, causing damage through ulceration, inflammation, and hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms of gastrointestinal infection arise either from toxin production during colonization (as with C. difficile) or from organisms that invade the mucosa and cause direct damage through ulceration, inflammation, and hemorrhage. Ulcers, hemorrhage, and organisms within the mucosa indicate the invasive mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of the normal microbiota facilitates colonization by other organisms but does not itself produce ulceration and hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of ciliary activity is a respiratory-tract mechanism, not a cause of colonic ulceration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A preformed toxin ingested in food produces rapid-onset vomiting and non-bloody diarrhea without organisms invading the mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superantigens cause massive cytokine release and systemic effects, not focal mucosal ulceration with tissue invasion.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: Within a few hours of eating potato salad and custard at a picnic, several attendees develop nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea. Stool cultures fail to grow the responsible organism. Which of the following best explains the rapid onset of illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disruption of the resident gut microbiota

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous spread of bacteria to the intestine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ingestion of heat-resistant toxin already formed in food

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invasion of the intestinal mucosa by the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid multiplication of the bacteria within the colon lumen

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal food poisoning is caused by preformed, heat-resistant enterotoxin, so disease occurs even without viable bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. aureus contaminates foods such as custards or potato salad, and its heat-resistant enterotoxin can survive cooking. Because the toxin is already present in the food, it causes rapid-onset vomiting and non-bloody diarrhea; the presence of toxin even in the absence of viable bacteria is sufficient to cause disease, which is why cultures may be negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Microbiota disruption underlies antibiotic-associated C. difficile infection, not food-borne intoxication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematogenous spread carries organisms to distant sites such as heart valves, not from food to the gut.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucosal invasion produces ulceration, inflammation, and hemorrhage, typically with bloody diarrhea rather than this picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Illness within hours is too fast to be explained by bacterial growth in the gut; the toxin was present before ingestion.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is recovering from influenza when she develops a new fever, productive cough, and lobar consolidation caused by a bacterial pathogen. Which of the following best explains her increased susceptibility to this second infection?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of the normal gut microbiota

explanation.summary: Airway damage from an influenza virus impairs local respiratory defenses and allows a superimposed bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Impairment of local immunity predisposes to infection of the respiratory tract. Clearance of pathogens by the mucociliary system can be hampered by smoking, and airway damage from an influenza virus may allow for a superimposed bacterial infection, as in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A breached epidermis predisposes to skin infection, not to a pulmonary infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gut microbiota depletion predisposes to C. difficile colitis, not to secondary pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric acidity protects the GI tract and is irrelevant to bacterial pneumonia after influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary obstruction is a susceptibility factor for urogenital infection.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student develops a prolonged cough and low-grade fever. The responsible organism is a bacterium that releases toxins into the airway, allowing it to persist despite normal mucus production. Which of the following is the most likely effect of these toxins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of complement by Lipid A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of desmoglein-1 in the airway epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disruption of the cytoskeleton of enterocytes

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae releases toxins that impair ciliary activity, limiting the respiratory tract's ability to remove the pathogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The respiratory tract traps particles in mucin and moves them with cilia to the back of the throat for clearance. Some bacteria, such as M. pneumoniae, release toxins that impair ciliary activity (ciliary immobility), limiting the ability to remove the pathogen from the airway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipid A is the immune-activating portion of gram-negative endotoxin, not a secreted ciliary toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmoglein-1 cleavage is the action of S. aureus exfoliative toxins on skin keratinocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytoskeletal disruption is caused by C. difficile toxins A and B in the colon.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of protein synthesis is the mechanism of diphtheria toxin's A component.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with a markedly enlarged prostate and incomplete bladder emptying develops recurrent urinary tract infections. Which of the following best explains his predisposition to these infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disruption of the normal gut microbiota

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of secretory IgA in the urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of the flushing action of urine flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced antimicrobial fatty acids on the perineal skin

explanation.summary: Urinary obstruction removes the flushing defense of urine flow and is a susceptibility factor for urogenital infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The flow of urine from the bladder washes away potential pathogens, so organisms must adhere to avoid being flushed out through the urethra. Obstruction, as with an enlarged prostate, is a susceptibility factor because it removes this flushing defense.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gut microbiota limits colonization of the GI tract and is not altered by prostatic obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peristalsis is the wave-like movement of the GI tract that prevents microbial overgrowth, not the urogenital defense at issue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgA antibodies are listed among the gastrointestinal defenses; the urogenital defense described is urine flow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antimicrobial fatty acids are a skin defense and are not the mechanism affected by outflow obstruction.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A newborn is found at birth to have cataracts, a rash, and developmental abnormalities. During pregnancy the mother had only a mild, self-limited febrile illness. Which of the following routes of transmission most likely produced the infant's findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exposure during passage through the birth canal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhalation of aerosolized droplets in the nursery

explanation.summary: TORCH pathogens cross the placenta to the fetus and cause developmental abnormalities, eye damage, and skin manifestations while maternal illness is mild.
explanation.whyCorrect: Placenta-fetal transmission is the common form of vertical infection for TORCH pathogens (Toxoplasmosis, Other such as syphilis, Rubella, CMV, and HSV). These commonly cause developmental abnormalities, eye damage, and skin manifestations while maternal signs and symptoms are often mild, exactly as described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Birth-canal exposure transmits N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, producing conjunctivitis after delivery rather than congenital developmental defects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal milk transmits viruses such as CMV, HIV, and HBV postnatally; it cannot account for abnormalities present at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Droplet inhalation is a postnatal person-to-person route and would not produce findings already present at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Umbilical inoculation is not a route of vertical transmission described for congenital eye and developmental defects.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A woman with a chronic viral infection delivers a healthy infant by cesarean section and asks whether she can breastfeed. Her physician explains that maternal milk can transmit her infection to the newborn. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen?

explanation.summary: Maternal milk may transmit certain viruses, including CMV, HIV, and hepatitis B virus, to the newborn.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to placenta-fetal transmission, maternal milk may transmit certain viruses to the newborn, such as CMV, HIV, and hepatitis B virus (HBV). Of the choices, only HBV is a chronic viral infection transmitted by this route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. trachomatis is contracted during passage through the birth canal and causes chlamydial conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. difficile is a hardy spore-forming gut pathogen spread on surfaces, not a milk-borne virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N. gonorrhoeae is acquired during passage through the birth canal, not through milk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoplasmosis is a TORCH pathogen transmitted across the placenta during gestation.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops a bacterial infection of a hand wound. Several days later he has tender, enlarged lymph nodes in the axilla, followed by fever and positive blood cultures. Which of the following best describes the sequence by which the organism reached his bloodstream?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adherence to urethral epithelium and ascent to the kidney

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct erosion from the lymph node into an adjacent artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ingestion by macrophages that carried it across the alveoli

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage through lymphatics to lymph nodes, then blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retrograde transport along peripheral nerves to the cord

explanation.summary: Pathogens may pass through the lymphatics to lymph nodes before gaining access to blood vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infectious agents spread beyond the initial site using lymphatics, blood vessels, and peripheral nerves. Bloodborne dissemination is common and efficient, and such pathogens may pass through the lymphatics to the lymph nodes before gaining access to the blood, which explains regional lymphadenopathy preceding bacteremia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urethral adherence and ascent describe urogenital infection, not spread from a skin wound.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Organisms in a draining node do not erode directly into an adjacent artery; entry into the blood occurs by lymphatic drainage into the venous system.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alveolar phagocytosis is a respiratory defense, unrelated to spread from a hand wound.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retrograde axonal transport is how certain viruses reach the CNS, and it does not produce lymphadenopathy or bacteremia.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a congenitally bicuspid aortic valve develops infective endocarditis after a transient bacteremia. Which of the following best explains why his valve was susceptible to bacterial attachment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endocardial damage from turbulent blood flow across the valve

choices.label: B
choices.text: Entry of oral bacteria through cuts in the gums

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired clearance of bacteria by alveolar phagocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intraoperative contamination at the time of valve placement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Introduction of skin bacteria by a hypodermic needle

explanation.summary: Congenital valve defects create turbulent flow that damages the endocardium and provides a nidus for bacterial attachment and vegetation formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital defects of the heart, such as a bicuspid aortic valve, cause turbulent blood flow, which damages the endocardium and provides a nidus for pathogen attachment and vegetation formation. Figure 2 of the brick shows friable vegetations on a congenitally bicuspid valve caused by S. aureus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gum cuts introducing oral bacteria explain a dental source of bacteremia, not the valve's intrinsic susceptibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alveolar phagocytosis is a respiratory defense and has no bearing on valvular susceptibility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intraoperative contamination is the mechanism for endocarditis of artificial heart valves, not a native bicuspid valve.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Needle introduction of skin bacteria is the IV drug use mechanism; it explains the bacteremia, not why this particular valve was vulnerable.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with a prosthetic mitral valve and poor dental hygiene develops fever and a new murmur two weeks after a tooth extraction. Blood cultures grow gram-negative coccobacilli. Which of the following best explains how these organisms reached her bloodstream?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspiration of oral secretions into the lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contamination of the valve during its surgical placement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Entry of oral bacteria through cuts in the gums

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inoculation of skin flora by an intravenous needle

explanation.summary: Poor dental health and dental procedures introduce oral bacteria, such as gram-negative coccobacilli, into the bloodstream via cuts in the gums.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poor dental health and dental procedures may introduce oral bacteria, such as gram-negative coccobacilli, into the bloodstream via cuts in the gums, which can then lead to endocarditis. The timing after a tooth extraction and the gram-negative coccobacilli point to a dental source.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspiration deposits organisms in the airway and would cause pneumonia rather than seeding a heart valve.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intraoperative contamination causes prosthetic valve endocarditis soon after surgery, not an infection with oral organisms two weeks after a dental procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Needle inoculation of skin flora is the mechanism in intravenous drug use, which is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intestinal translocation is not the route described for oral coccobacilli after dental work.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman develops a painful, vesicular rash confined to a single dermatome. The responsible virus had remained latent after a childhood infection and traveled along a peripheral nerve. Which of the following viruses is known to spread to and from the nervous system by retrograde axonal transport?

explanation.summary: Rabies virus, poliovirus, varicella-zoster virus, and HSV spread along nerves by retrograde axonal transport.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viruses may spread along nerves to the central nervous system, a phenomenon known as retrograde axonal transport. The viruses that use this route include rabies virus, poliovirus, varicella-zoster virus (VZV), and HSV; a dermatomal vesicular rash reflects VZV involvement of a sensory nerve.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatitis A is a fecal-oral pathogen and is not described as spreading along nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV causes proliferative verrucous warts in epithelium and does not travel along nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Influenza virus is an airway pathogen spread by aerosolized droplets, not by neural transport.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rubella is a TORCH pathogen transmitted across the placenta, not a neurotropic virus using axonal transport.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A nurse finishes caring for a hospitalized patient with C. difficile diarrhea. Which of the following is the most appropriate hand-hygiene measure before moving to the next patient?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Washing the hands with soap and water

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wiping the hands with a dry paper towel

explanation.summary: C. difficile spores resist alcohol-based handrubs, so hands should be washed with soap and water after probable contact.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. difficile is hardy and survives for months on surfaces due to spore formation, the spore being the dormant form of the pathogen. These spores require special disinfectants to neutralize and are resistant to alcohol-based handrubs, so medical professionals are encouraged to wash their hands with soap and water following probable contact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Air-drying alone removes nothing and leaves spores on the hands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Repeating an alcohol handrub does not overcome the spores' resistance to alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alcohol-based handrubs do not neutralize C. difficile spores regardless of contact time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A dry towel does not remove or inactivate spores.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: During an outbreak of a coronavirus respiratory illness, public health officials note that the virus can infect people standing more than six feet from an infected person and can remain suspended in indoor air for extended periods. Which of the following modes of transmission best accounts for these observations?

explanation.summary: Small aerosolized droplets can travel beyond six feet and remain airborne for extended periods, infecting the respiratory system.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aerosolized droplets are a route of person-to-person transmission for pathogens infecting the respiratory system. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates that COVID-19 virus, a coronavirus, can spread in small droplets through the air at a distance greater than six feet and remain airborne for extended periods of time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fecal-oral spread involves ingestion of contaminated food or water and does not explain airborne infection at a distance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sexual transmission requires mucosal contact and cannot occur across a room.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vector transmission requires a bite from an insect or animal, not airborne suspension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertical transmission is mother-to-fetus spread and is unrelated to indoor air.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man develops high fever, hypotension, a diffuse rash with subsequent desquamation, and multiorgan dysfunction five days after nasal surgery. His nasal packing has not been changed. Which of the following best explains his systemic illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A-B toxin inhibiting myocardial protein synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of desmoglein-1 in the epidermis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heat-resistant enterotoxin absorbed from the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipid A of endotoxin activating complement cascades

explanation.summary: Toxic shock syndrome results from superantigen toxins and can follow infected nasal packing or post-operative wound-care materials, not only tampon use.
explanation.whyCorrect: Superantigen toxins may cause toxic shock syndrome as a consequence of massive cytokine release, producing desquamation, hypotension, and multiorgan effects. TSS is not limited to S. aureus or tampon use; it may be seen secondary to superantigenic toxins produced by Streptococcus pyogenes, or result from infected nasal packing or post-operative wound-care materials.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An A-B toxin inhibiting protein synthesis describes diphtheria toxin, which produces a pharyngeal pseudomembrane and myocarditis rather than desquamation and shock after nasal packing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmoglein-1 cleavage causes staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, a blistering illness primarily of children, not hypotension and multiorgan dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enterotoxin acts on the GI tract to cause rapid vomiting and diarrhea after ingestion, and there is no food exposure here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipid A endotoxin drives gram-negative septic shock but does not produce the desquamating rash of a superantigen syndrome.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with a diffuse maculopapular rash including the palms and soles undergoes skin biopsy. The dermis shows an infiltrate surrounding blood vessels composed of small cells with a single round purple nucleus and minimal surrounding cytoplasm; no neutrophils or granulomas are seen. Which of the following types of organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: A perivascular lymphocytic (mononuclear) infiltrate is the tissue reaction to spirochetes such as T. pallidum in secondary syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphocytic inflammation is seen in response to viruses, intracellular bacteria, intracellular parasites, helminths, and bacterial spirochetes such as T. pallidum. In secondary syphilis a mononuclear infiltrate of lymphocytes surrounds vessels, and histologically a lymphocyte is identified by its single purple nucleus with minimal surrounding cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mycoplasma is described for its ciliary toxin in the airway, not a perivascular lymphocytic dermatitis with palm and sole rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyogenic cocci produce suppurative inflammation dominated by neutrophils, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C. diphtheriae causes toxin-mediated tissue necrosis and a pharyngeal pseudomembrane rather than a lymphocytic rash.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Foreign material elicits granulomatous inflammation, and no granulomas are present.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A researcher engineers a mutant diphtheria toxin in which the B component is nonfunctional while the A component is intact. When cultured human cells are exposed to the mutant toxin, which of the following is the most likely result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells die by an alternative pathway independent of the ribosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytokine release is exaggerated because binding is unopposed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein synthesis is inhibited but no fibrin is deposited

choices.label: D
choices.text: The toxin enters the cells but cannot reach the nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The toxin fails to enter the cells and they survive

explanation.summary: In an A-B toxin the B component is responsible for binding and delivery of the toxin into the host cell by endocytosis; without it the active A component cannot enter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diphtheria toxin is an A-B toxin: the A component is responsible for the toxicity, while the B component is responsible for binding and delivery of the toxin into the host cell by endocytosis. The B component initiates entry into the cell via an endocytic vacuole, after which the A component inhibits protein synthesis in the ribosome. A nonfunctional B component therefore prevents entry, and the cells are spared.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The toxin has no alternative, ribosome-independent mechanism of killing cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytokine release describes superantigens; diphtheria toxin does not act by unopposed binding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The A component cannot inhibit ribosomal protein synthesis if it is never delivered into the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The toxin cannot enter without the B component, and its target is the ribosome, not the nucleus.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with a long history of injecting crushed oral tablets intravenously has lung nodules. Biopsy shows collections of activated macrophages and multinucleated giant cells surrounding refractile crystalline material, with no organisms identified on special stains. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this reaction?

explanation.summary: Granulomatous inflammation can occur around foreign material such as talc introduced by intravenous drug use.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apart from infections, granulomatous inflammation may occur in the context of foreign material, such as talc or other material introduced from intravenous drug use, as well as certain autoimmune diseases and sarcoidosis. Crystalline material within macrophage and giant cell aggregates in an injection drug user points to a foreign-body granuloma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spirochetes elicit a lymphocytic mononuclear infiltrate rather than a foreign-body granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune diseases can cause granulomas but would not explain refractile crystalline material in an injection drug user.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycobacteria produce caseating granulomas and organisms would be expected on special stains; none are present, and crystalline material points elsewhere.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease of unknown etiology and is a diagnosis of exclusion; an identifiable foreign material excludes it.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 29-year-old Black woman presents with dyspnea and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows well-formed granulomas without central necrosis. The physician suspects a granulomatous disease of unknown etiology that is more common in young adults. Which of the following must be done before this diagnosis can be established?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Culture of pyogenic bacteria from the node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Demonstration of Lipid A endotoxin in serum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exclusion of tuberculosis and other causes

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion; tuberculosis and other causes of granulomatous inflammation must be eliminated first.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sarcoidosis, a granulomatous disease of unknown etiology, often manifests in hilar lymph nodes and lung parenchyma, occurs in young adults, and is more common in Black women compared to Caucasians. Before the diagnosis is made, tuberculosis and other causes must be eliminated from the differential through appropriate investigation, because the histologic pattern alone is not specific.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyogenic bacteria produce suppurative inflammation, not granulomas, so culturing them is not the required step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipid A is the immune-activating portion of gram-negative endotoxin and has no role in diagnosing a granulomatous disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-toxin antibodies are relevant to diphtheria toxin, not to hilar granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intranuclear inclusions characterize the cytopathic pattern of viral infection, not granulomatous disease.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has several rough, raised, warty growths on her fingers. Biopsy shows marked proliferation of squamous epithelium without neutrophils, granulomas, or necrosis. Which of the following histologic patterns of reaction does this lesion represent?

explanation.summary: Some viruses, such as HPV, cause cells to proliferate, producing verrucous warts as part of the cytopathic-cytoproliferative pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cytopathic-cytoproliferative pattern is caused by viruses replicating within cells. In addition to cytopathic changes such as inclusions and multinucleation, some viruses can cause cells to proliferate, such as the verrucous warts of human papilloma virus (HPV), which is what epithelial proliferation without inflammation or necrosis represents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic inflammation and scarring is a fibrotic response to longstanding insult, not a proliferative epithelial wart.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomatous inflammation features aggregates of macrophages and giant cells, not proliferating epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Suppurative inflammation is dominated by neutrophils and pus, which are absent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue necrosis is cell death, whereas this lesion shows cell proliferation.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops a cluster of painful fluid-filled vesicles on his lip. A scraping from the base of a vesicle shows enlarged, multinucleated cells with nuclear molding and margination of chromatin. Which of the following best explains the formation of the fluid-filled blisters?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fusion of activated macrophages into giant cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Toxin-mediated cleavage of desmoglein-1 in keratinocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral damage detaching epithelium with serous effusion

explanation.summary: In viral cytopathic infections such as HSV, cell damage causes detachment of epithelium and serous effusion, resulting in blisters.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cytopathic changes of HSV include multinucleation, nuclear molding, and nuclear margination seen inside infected cells. Cell damage from the virus may also cause detachment of the epithelium and serous effusion, resulting in blisters, which accounts for the vesicles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrin deposition forming a pseudomembrane is the diphtheria toxin reaction in the throat.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Giant cells from macrophage fusion belong to granulomatous inflammation; the multinucleated cells here are virus-infected epithelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophil accumulation with liquefaction describes pus and abscess formation by pyogenic bacteria, not viral vesicles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Desmoglein-1 cleavage by staphylococcal exfoliative toxin causes scalded-skin syndrome, not the HSV cytopathic findings shown.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a 30-year history of hepatitis B virus infection develops ascites and a small, nodular liver on imaging. Biopsy shows dense bands of fibrosis with a lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following histologic patterns of reaction to infection is represented?

explanation.summary: Longstanding hepatitis B infection produces chronic inflammation and scarring, culminating in cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: When tissues are unable to heal under a longstanding insult, scarring occurs, usually associated with chronic inflammation, a type of lymphocytic mononuclear inflammation. Longstanding hepatitis B virus infection results in dense fibrosis of the liver, known as cirrhosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseating necrosis is the central necrosis of tuberculous granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The cytopathic-cytoproliferative pattern refers to inclusions, multinucleation, or proliferation in infected cells rather than end-stage fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomatous inflammation consists of macrophage aggregates and giant cells, which are not described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppurative inflammation is an acute neutrophil-rich reaction to pyogenic bacteria, not decades of fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A pediatrician administers a routine childhood vaccine that protects against diphtheria. Which of the following best describes the active component of this vaccine and the protection it produces?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formalin-inactivated toxin that elicits anti-toxin antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Horse-serum antibodies that neutralize circulating toxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Killed whole bacteria that induce anti-cell-wall antibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Live attenuated C. diphtheriae that colonizes the pharynx

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purified B component that blocks toxin receptors

explanation.summary: The diphtheria vaccine uses toxoid, a formalin-inactivated form of diphtheria toxin, to generate an anti-toxin antibody response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-toxin antibodies are generated against diphtheria toxin (DT). Today, the diphtheria vaccine utilizes toxoid, a formalin-inactivated form of DT toxin, which generates an anti-toxin antibody response in the recipient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Horse-serum anti-DT antibodies describe the historical diphtheria antitoxin used for treatment (as in the 1925 Nome serum run), not the vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protection derives from antibodies against the toxin rather than against bacterial cell wall components.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vaccine does not contain live organisms; protection targets the toxin, not colonization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vaccine is an inactivated whole toxin (toxoid), not an isolated B component acting as a receptor blocker.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman reports several months of pain in her wrists, hands, elbows, and knees that improves with ibuprofen but never fully resolves. She has a red rash across both cheeks and the bridge of her nose, along with painful oral ulcers. Her temperature is 39.1 C (102.4 F). Laboratory studies show a decreased white blood cell count, hemoglobin, and platelet count. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A young woman with a malar (butterfly) rash, arthritis, oral ulcers, and pancytopenia has systemic lupus erythematosus.
explanation.whyCorrect: SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease that classically affects young women and presents with a butterfly-shaped malar rash, arthritis, oral/nasopharyngeal ulcers, and pancytopenia from autoantibodies that opsonize blood cells. Its features are summarized by the mnemonic RASH OR PAIN.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Goodpasture syndrome affects the lungs and kidneys with hemoptysis and glomerulonephritis, not a malar rash and arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with sinus, lung, and kidney disease, not a malar rash with oral ulcers and arthralgias in this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is a childhood disease with palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, and arthralgias.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetric joint swelling of the hands and feet but does not produce a malar rash or pancytopenia.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a several-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus is evaluated with echocardiography. Imaging reveals small, single and multiple warty vegetations distributed on the surfaces of the mitral valve leaflets. Blood cultures are repeatedly negative. Which of the following best describes this cardiac finding?

explanation.summary: Sterile warty vegetations on the valve surface in a lupus patient are Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a nonbacterial verrucous endocarditis of SLE that produces small single or multiple warty deposits distinctively on the surface of the valve leaflets. Because it is immune-mediated rather than infectious, blood cultures are negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granulomatous vasculitis is a feature of granulomatosis with polyangiitis affecting small vessels, not sterile valve vegetations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vegetations in infective endocarditis are considerably larger, contain infectious organisms, and would be associated with positive blood cultures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vegetations in rheumatic heart disease are smaller and are confined to the lines of closure of the leaflets, not scattered on the leaflet surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid nodules occur in subcutaneous tissue in rheumatoid arthritis, not as valvular vegetations.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a platelet count of 38,000/mm3 and scattered petechiae. Peripheral smear shows no schistocytes. Which of the following best explains the low platelet count in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies against the platelet basement membrane collagen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deficiency of ADAMTS13 causing platelet consumption in microthrombi

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgA immune complexes depositing in the marrow

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia in SLE results from anti-platelet glycoprotein antibodies that mark platelets for splenic macrophage removal.
explanation.whyCorrect: In SLE, autoantibodies bind platelet membrane glycoproteins, leading to removal of the opsonized platelets by macrophages, particularly in the sinusoids of the spleen. This immune thrombocytopenia is the most common cytopenia mechanism described in lupus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-basement membrane collagen antibodies are the mechanism of Goodpasture syndrome, not lupus thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow granulomas are not a described mechanism of the pancytopenia of SLE, which is antibody-mediated opsonization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with schistocytes, which are absent here and are not the lupus mechanism taught.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA immune complex deposition characterizes Henoch-Schonlein purpura, not SLE-related platelet destruction.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops pleuritic chest pain and glomerular injury. Her disease is understood to result from antigen-antibody aggregates that deposit in tissues and activate complement, driving widespread inflammation. This process is an example of which of the following hypersensitivity reactions?

explanation.summary: SLE is a type III hypersensitivity reaction driven by immune-complex deposition and complement activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes SLE as due to a type III hypersensitivity reaction in which immune complexes deposit in tissue and activate complement, leading to widespread inflammation of the skin, serosa, kidney, and other organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I reactions are IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity such as anaphylaxis, not the immune-complex disease of lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type II reactions involve antibodies directed against fixed cell-surface antigens; SLE inflammation is attributed to circulating immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type IV reactions are delayed and T-cell mediated, whereas lupus tissue injury here is complement-activating immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type V receptor-stimulating hypersensitivity describes diseases like Graves disease, not lupus.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is being worked up for suspected systemic lupus erythematosus. An antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is positive. Which of the following additional antibodies is most specific for confirming the diagnosis of SLE?

explanation.summary: After a positive ANA, anti-dsDNA (or anti-Smith) antibodies help confirm systemic lupus erythematosus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ANA test is usually the initial screen, and if positive, sub-serologies are checked. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are specific for SLE and are used to confirm the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-CCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis, found in about 70% of early cases, not for SLE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody is the hallmark of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid factor is seen in rheumatoid arthritis and is nonspecific, appearing in other diseases as well.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with several months of symmetric swelling and morning stiffness of the small joints of her hands is suspected of having rheumatoid arthritis. Positivity for which of the following antibodies is most specific for this diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-CCP antibodies are found in about 70% of patients with early rheumatoid arthritis and are highly specific for the disease, unlike rheumatoid factor which is nonspecific.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-dsDNA is found in systemic lupus erythematosus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody is seen in Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) is seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid factor is present in 75-80% of RA patients but is not specific because it appears in other diseases such as SLE.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has progressive destruction of the joints of her hands. Biopsy of an affected joint shows an expanding mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over and erodes the articular cartilage. Which of the following terms best describes this lesion?

explanation.summary: The proliferative synovial mass that erodes articular cartilage in RA is called a pannus.
explanation.whyCorrect: In rheumatoid arthritis, the inflamed synovium becomes edematous, thickened, and hyperplastic, forming a pannus, a mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over and causes erosion of the articular cartilage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A generic granuloma does not describe the specific proliferative synovial tissue of RA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A rheumatoid nodule is a subcutaneous lesion with central fibrinoid necrosis and palisading macrophages, not the intra-articular mass eroding cartilage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A tophus is a deposit of urate crystals seen in gout, not rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A verrucous vegetation refers to the valvular lesions of Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis of the hands and wrists and a positive anti-CCP antibody has a firm subcutaneous nodule on the extensor surface of his forearm near the elbow. Biopsy shows a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a rim of activated macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A subcutaneous nodule with central fibrinoid necrosis rimmed by palisading macrophages in an RA patient is a rheumatoid nodule.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rheumatoid nodules are an infrequent manifestation of RA that occur in subcutaneous tissue of the forearm, elbow, occiput, and lumbosacral area. Microscopically they show a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a rim of activated macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Goodpasture pulmonary lesion is intra-alveolar hemorrhage with hemosiderin-laden macrophages, not a subcutaneous nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A gouty tophaceous nodule contains urate crystals, not a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis with palisading macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Henoch-Schonlein lesions are palpable purpura from IgA immune complexes, not fibrinoid-necrosis nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Libman-Sacks vegetations are sterile warty deposits on heart valves, not subcutaneous nodules.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presents with cough productive of blood and patchy consolidations on chest imaging, followed within weeks by hematuria and rising creatinine. Renal biopsy shows crescent formation in Bowman capsule with linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. Autoantibodies in this patient are most likely directed against which of the following?

explanation.summary: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by autoantibodies against type IV collagen in the basement membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Goodpasture syndrome occurs in the teens or twenties, more often in males, and is caused by circulating autoantibodies against type IV collagen found in the basement membrane. This produces linear IgG on the glomerular basement membrane, crescentic glomerulonephritis, and alveolar hemorrhage with hemoptysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies are specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are the marker of systemic lupus erythematosus, not Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-platelet glycoprotein antibodies cause the immune thrombocytopenia of SLE.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA) characterize granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is diagnosed with Goodpasture syndrome after presenting with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Which of the following treatments most directly targets the underlying cause of his disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allopurinol to lower the serum urate concentration in gout

choices.label: B
choices.text: Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for valvular vegetations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral iron supplementation for chronic alveolar blood loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasmapheresis to remove anti-basement membrane antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic anticoagulation to prevent microthrombi in small vessels

explanation.summary: Goodpasture syndrome is treated with plasmapheresis to remove the pathogenic anti-basement membrane antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The prognosis of Goodpasture syndrome has been markedly improved with plasmapheresis, in which the anti-basement membrane antibodies are removed from the plasma, directly addressing the antibody-mediated lung and kidney injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allopurinol lowers urate in gout and has no role in Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibiotics treat infective endocarditis, not the sterile autoimmune injury of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron supplementation does not address the causative autoantibodies even though alveolar hemorrhage occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticoagulation targets thrombosis and does not remove the anti-basement membrane antibodies.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has months of fever, fatigue, and weight loss along with chronic sinusitis, bloody nasal discharge, and a saddle-nose deformity. He now has hemoptysis and gross hematuria. Biopsy of a lung nodule shows necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and vessel wall injury. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: The triad of upper airway, lung, and kidney disease with necrotizing granulomas is granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis with the classic triad of upper respiratory tract, lung, and kidney disease. Findings include bloody nasal discharge, saddle-nose deformity, lung nodules with hemoptysis, and hematuria, and biopsy shows necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Goodpasture syndrome affects only the lungs and kidneys with linear IgG and lacks sinus disease and granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is a childhood IgA disease with purpura and abdominal pain, not necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatoid arthritis is a joint disease and does not cause this upper-airway and renal granulomatous triad.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SLE presents with malar rash, arthritis, and multisystem immune-complex disease rather than necrotizing airway granulomas and saddle-nose deformity.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy develops palpable purpuric skin lesions over the extensor surfaces of his legs and his buttocks, along with colicky abdominal pain, arthralgias, and microscopic hematuria. Skin biopsy immunofluorescence is most likely to reveal deposition of which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgA immune complexes with complement C3

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgM rheumatoid factor in synovial tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linear IgG along the basement membrane

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura in a child is caused by deposition of IgA immune complexes with complement C3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Henoch-Schonlein purpura occurs most commonly in children 3-8 years old with purpuric skin lesions on extensor surfaces and buttocks, abdominal pain, arthralgias, and renal abnormalities. Like SLE it results from immune-complex deposition, usually IgA with IgG and complement (C3).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are markers of systemic lupus erythematosus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgM rheumatoid factor is found in rheumatoid arthritis, not in the purpuric lesions of HSP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linear IgG along the basement membrane is the immunofluorescence pattern of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PR3-ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not HSP.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is told that her new diagnosis is an autoimmune disease. She asks what has gone wrong in her immune system. Which of the following best describes the fundamental defect underlying autoimmune disease?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive production of regulatory T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of neutrophils to phagocytose bacteria

explanation.summary: Autoimmunity results from loss of self-tolerance, so the immune system attacks normal cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmunity comes into play when the immune system loses the ability to recognize and then ignore self-antigens. This loss of self-tolerance leads the body to destroy normal cells because it can no longer distinguish normal from abnormal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement is activated, not absent, in immune-complex autoimmune diseases such as SLE.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Regulatory T cells restrain immune responses; an excess would suppress rather than cause autoimmunity, and this is not the defect described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of bacterial phagocytosis describes an immunodeficiency, not the loss of tolerance that defines autoimmunity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoimmune diseases such as SLE involve abundant autoantibody production, not an inability to make antibodies.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss and is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus, an organ-specific autoimmune disease. The immune response in this patient is directed against which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Myelin in the central nervous system

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type IV collagen in basement membranes

explanation.summary: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is an organ-specific autoimmune disease targeting pancreatic beta cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: In some autoimmune diseases the immune response is directed against a single organ or tissue, producing organ-specific disease. Type 1 diabetes mellitus targets the beta cells of the pancreas, in contrast to systemic diseases like SLE that affect multiple organ systems.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Liver cells are targeted in autoimmune hepatitis, not type 1 diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myelin in the central nervous system is the target in multiple sclerosis, another organ-specific autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Synovial involvement characterizes rheumatoid arthritis, a systemic autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV collagen in basement membranes is the target in Goodpasture syndrome.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with fatigue, joint pain, and an erythematous rash over her cheeks undergoes a skin biopsy. H&E staining shows liquefactive degeneration of the basal layer of the epidermis and edema at the dermoepidermal junction. Immunofluorescence of the biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central fibrinoid necrosis with palisaded macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granular IgG deposits at the basement membrane zone

explanation.summary: Skin involvement in SLE shows basal-layer liquefactive degeneration on H&E and IgG deposits along the dermoepidermal junction on immunofluorescence.
explanation.whyCorrect: In SLE involving the skin, an H&E stained section shows liquefactive degeneration of the basal layer of the epidermis and edema at the dermoepidermal junction, while immunofluorescence stained for IgG reveals deposits of IgG along the dermoepidermal junction, reflecting immune-complex deposition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central fibrinoid necrosis rimmed by palisaded macrophages describes a rheumatoid nodule of rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages reflect previous hemorrhage in the lungs of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesangial IgA deposition is the renal immunofluorescence finding of Henoch-Schonlein purpura, not a skin finding in lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated giant cells are seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not in lupus skin.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is brought to the emergency department after a generalized seizure. Over the preceding weeks her family noted paranoid thoughts and auditory hallucinations. Which of the following best explains these neuropsychiatric manifestations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies crossing the blood-brain barrier and reacting with neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granulomatous vasculitis of the cerebral arteries and arterioles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Opsonization of circulating platelets causing intracranial hemorrhage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sterile warty vegetations embolizing from the mitral valve leaflets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uremic encephalopathy from progressive renal failure and azotemia

explanation.summary: Psychosis and seizures in SLE are attributed to antibodies that cross the blood-brain barrier and react with neurons or neurotransmitter receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the manifestations of SLE are psychosis and seizures, a phenomenon attributed to antibodies that cross the blood-brain barrier and react with neurons or with receptors for various neurotransmitters; cytokines may also play a role.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatous vasculitis is the lesion of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not the mechanism of lupus psychosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-platelet antibodies cause thrombocytopenia in SLE, but the neuropsychiatric phenomena are attributed to direct antibody reactions with neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Libman-Sacks vegetations are a valvular manifestation of SLE, but the neuropsychiatric symptoms are attributed to antibody effects on neurons, not embolization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uremia is the most common cause of death in Goodpasture syndrome; it is not the explanation given for lupus psychosis and seizures.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with long-standing systemic lupus erythematosus develops fever, chills, and a new heart murmur. Echocardiography shows a large vegetation on the mitral valve, and multiple blood cultures grow organisms. Which of the following best characterizes this valvular lesion?

explanation.summary: Large vegetations that contain organisms indicate infective endocarditis, unlike the small sterile warty deposits of Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vegetations in infective endocarditis are considerably larger than those of Libman-Sacks endocarditis and contain infectious organisms, consistent with the positive blood cultures and fever in this patient. A lupus history does not make every valvular lesion Libman-Sacks disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune-complex inflammation underlies SLE but does not produce a large vegetation containing organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Libman-Sacks endocarditis produces small single or multiple warty, non-bacterial deposits on the leaflet surface, so cultures would be negative and the vegetations small.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vegetations in rheumatic heart disease are smaller and confined to the lines of closure of the leaflets and are not infectious.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid nodules are subcutaneous lesions of rheumatoid arthritis, not culture-positive valvular vegetations.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: Most systemic autoimmune diseases predominantly affect women. Which of the following autoimmune diseases instead exhibits a male predominance?

explanation.summary: Goodpasture syndrome, unlike most autoimmune diseases, shows a male predominance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Goodpasture syndrome is an uncommon autoimmune disease occurring most often in patients in their teens or 20s, and in contrast to most other autoimmune conditions it exhibits a male predominance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hepatitis is an organ-specific autoimmune disease and is not singled out as male-predominant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple sclerosis is an organ-specific disease targeting myelin and is not described as male-predominant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatoid arthritis follows the usual female predominance of autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SLE predominantly affects women, as illustrated by the typical young female patient with malar rash.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has warm, swollen metacarpophalangeal joints. Synovial fluid analysis shows abundant inflammatory cytokines. In rheumatoid arthritis, the cytokines that drive joint inflammation are secreted mainly by which of the following cells?

explanation.summary: Inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis is induced by cytokines secreted mainly by CD4+ helper T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pathologic changes in RA are due to antibodies against self antigens and inflammation induced by cytokines, mainly those secreted by CD4+ helper T cells. Th17 and Th1 cells responding to self antigens, together with antibodies, enter the joint and activate the processes that lead to pannus formation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells are not identified as the principal cytokine source in RA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells mediate IgE-driven immediate hypersensitivity, not the T-cell cytokine inflammation of RA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are present in the joint but are not the main source of the cytokines that induce RA inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells produce antibodies such as rheumatoid factor, but the cytokine-driven inflammation is attributed mainly to CD4+ T cells.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with symmetric polyarthritis of the hands tests positive for rheumatoid factor. Which of the following best describes the structure and target of rheumatoid factor?

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG antibody against type IV collagen

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgM antibody against the Fc portion of IgG

explanation.summary: Rheumatoid factor is an IgM autoantibody directed against the Fc portion of IgG.
explanation.whyCorrect: RA is commonly associated with rheumatoid factor, an immunoglobulin M (IgM) autoantibody against the Fc portion of IgG, as well as anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rheumatoid factor is not an IgA antibody, and its target is IgG rather than collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies against citrullinated peptides are the anti-CCP antibodies, a separate RA-associated autoantibody, not rheumatoid factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies against proteinase 3 are the PR3-ANCAs of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against type IV collagen cause Goodpasture syndrome.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with an established diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus is found to have a positive rheumatoid factor on routine laboratory testing. She has no joint swelling or morning stiffness. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rheumatoid factor is nonspecific and also occurs in lupus

choices.label: B
choices.text: She has developed concurrent rheumatoid arthritis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The diagnosis of lupus should be revised to rheumatoid arthritis

choices.label: E
