choices.text: The result indicates anti-CCP antibodies are also present

explanation.summary: Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but not specific for RA and can be seen in other diseases such as SLE.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rheumatoid factor autoantibodies are seen in 75-80% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, but they are not specific because they can be seen in other diseases like SLE. A positive rheumatoid factor in a lupus patient without joint findings therefore does not establish rheumatoid arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Without the swollen, warm, painful joints of RA, a nonspecific rheumatoid factor does not establish a second diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Her lupus diagnosis is not overturned by rheumatoid factor, which is known to occur in SLE.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is diagnosed by valvular vegetations, not by rheumatoid factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-CCP is a separate, more specific antibody; rheumatoid factor positivity does not imply its presence.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man who has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years develops rheumatoid arthritis with high-titer anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies. Environmental factors such as smoking are thought to contribute to his disease by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of IgA immune complexes in synovium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct toxic destruction of articular cartilage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzymatic modification of self proteins by citrullination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generation of antibodies against type IV collagen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Induction of new HLA susceptibility genes

explanation.summary: Environmental factors such as smoking promote enzymatic citrullination of self proteins, creating the antigens recognized in RA.
explanation.whyCorrect: RA develops from a combined effect of genetic and environmental factors. Environmental factors such as infection and smoking lead to enzymatic modification (citrullination) of self protein, while susceptibility genes such as HLA cause failure of tolerance and unregulated lymphocyte activation; together these drive T and B cell responses to self antigens, including antigens in joint tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA immune-complex deposition characterizes Henoch-Schonlein purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cartilage erosion in RA is caused by the pannus, not by direct toxic injury from smoke.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against type IV collagen are the mechanism of Goodpasture syndrome, not RA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA susceptibility genes are inherited; environmental factors do not induce them but act alongside them.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis undergoes synovial biopsy of the knee. Histology shows synovial cell hyperplasia, dense inflammatory infiltrates forming lymphoid follicles, increased vascularity, and fibrinopurulent exudate on the synovial surface. Radiographs show erosion of bone adjacent to the joint. Which of the following best accounts for the bone loss?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of urate crystals in bone

explanation.summary: Bone breakdown in rheumatoid arthritis reflects osteoclastic activity in subchondral bone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Characteristic histologic features of RA include synovial cell hyperplasia, dense inflammatory infiltrates that frequently form lymphoid follicles, increased vascularity, fibrinopurulent exudate on the synovial and joint surface, and osteoclastic (bone breakdown) activity in subchondral bone. Together these changes produce the pannus that erodes articular cartilage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement-mediated cell lysis is not the described mechanism of bone loss in RA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Urate crystal deposition characterizes gout, not the synovitis of rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Necrotizing granulomas with giant cells are seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not in RA synovium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small-vessel vasculitis is the lesion of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not the cause of periarticular bone loss in RA.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man is diagnosed with Goodpasture syndrome after presenting with hemoptysis followed by rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. His family asks about the greatest threat to his life. Which of the following is the most common cause of death in this disease?

explanation.summary: Uremia is the most common cause of death in Goodpasture syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Goodpasture syndrome, glomerulonephritis rapidly progresses to renal failure, and the most common cause of death is uremia, a buildup of toxins like urea and creatinine due to the inability of the kidneys to filter waste from the blood. Prognosis has been markedly improved with plasmapheresis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infective endocarditis is not a feature of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intestinal bleeding is a feature of Henoch-Schonlein purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombocytopenia from anti-platelet antibodies is a manifestation of SLE, not Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although the disease usually begins with hemoptysis and lung consolidations, the most common cause of death is uremia rather than pulmonary hemorrhage.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man is diagnosed with Goodpasture syndrome. In the typical course of this disease, which of the following manifestations is most likely to have appeared first?

explanation.summary: Goodpasture syndrome usually begins with respiratory symptoms such as hemoptysis before renal manifestations develop.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most cases of Goodpasture syndrome begin with respiratory symptoms, such as hemoptysis (coughing up blood) and focal lung consolidations on imaging. Soon afterward, manifestations of glomerulonephritis appear and rapidly progress to renal failure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Palpable purpura characterizes Henoch-Schonlein purpura, not Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal failure develops after the initial respiratory phase, as glomerulonephritis progresses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Saddle-nose deformity results from the upper respiratory involvement of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symmetric small-joint arthritis is the presentation of rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with several weeks of hemoptysis undergoes lung biopsy. Sections show acute intra-alveolar hemorrhage and numerous macrophages whose cytoplasm stains blue with a Prussian blue stain. Serum contains antibodies against type IV collagen. The blue-staining material in the macrophages represents which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ingested fragments of type IV collagen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron from degraded red blood cells

explanation.summary: Prussian blue highlights hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which reflect previous alveolar hemorrhage in Goodpasture syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lung in Goodpasture syndrome shows acute intra-alveolar hemorrhage and hemosiderin-laden macrophages that reflect previous hemorrhage. The macrophages are highlighted blue by the Prussian blue iron stain because they contain iron recovered from degraded red blood cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prussian blue is an iron stain; it does not mark calcification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Citrullinated proteins are the antigens recognized by anti-CCP antibodies in rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type IV collagen is the antibody target in Goodpasture syndrome, but Prussian blue stains iron, not collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA immune complexes deposit in Henoch-Schonlein purpura and are not what Prussian blue detects.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic sinusitis, pulmonary nodules, and hematuria has serum antibodies against proteinase 3. Which of the following best describes how these antibodies produce vascular injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They activate neutrophils that interact with endothelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind type IV collagen in vessel basement membranes

choices.label: C
choices.text: They cross-link IgE on mast cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: They form circulating immune complexes that deposit in vessel walls

choices.label: E
choices.text: They opsonize endothelial cells for splenic removal

explanation.summary: PR3-ANCAs activate neutrophils, which interact with endothelial cells to cause microvascular damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is caused by antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies, specifically antibodies to proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA). PR3-ANCAs activate neutrophils and cause them to interact with endothelial cells in the vascular wall, leading to microvascular damage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding of type IV collagen in basement membranes is the mechanism of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells is the type I hypersensitivity mechanism, unrelated to ANCA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune-complex deposition is the type III mechanism of SLE and Henoch-Schonlein purpura, not the neutrophil activation of GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opsonization for splenic removal describes anti-platelet antibodies in SLE, not ANCA-mediated vasculitis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A laboratory report for a 46-year-old man with bloody nasal discharge and hemoptysis reads positive for c-ANCA. The antigen recognized by this antibody, for which it is now named, is which of the following?

explanation.summary: c-ANCA is now designated PR3-ANCA because its target is neutrophil proteinase 3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is caused by antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies, specifically antibodies to proteinase 3, termed PR3-ANCA and previously called c-ANCA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyclic citrullinated peptide is the target of anti-CCP antibodies in rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Double-stranded DNA is the target of anti-dsDNA antibodies in SLE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Fc portion of IgG is the target of rheumatoid factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV collagen is the target of the anti-basement membrane antibodies of Goodpasture syndrome.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Across patients with this disease, which of the following is the most common single finding?

explanation.summary: Upper respiratory tract findings are the most common single finding in granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nasal, sinus, or oral inflammation in GPA leads to purulent or bloody nasal discharge, saddle nose deformity, or oral ulcers. These upper respiratory findings are the most common single finding in GPA, ahead of the lung and kidney components of the classic triad.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nonspecific symptoms such as fever, fatigue, joint pains, and weight loss occur only sometimes and are not the most common single finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nephritic syndrome with edema and hematuria may develop but is less common than upper respiratory involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Petechiae and purpuric lesions may appear on the skin but are not the most frequent finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lung nodules, infiltrates, or cavities causing dyspnea and hemoptysis are part of the triad but are not the most common single finding.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with granulomatosis with polyangiitis develops periorbital and lower-extremity edema, gross hematuria, and a rising serum creatinine. Which of the following renal syndromes has most likely developed?

explanation.summary: The kidneys in GPA may develop nephritic syndrome, producing edema and sometimes gross hematuria.
explanation.whyCorrect: As part of the classic triad of upper respiratory tract, lung, and kidney disease, the kidneys in granulomatosis with polyangiitis may develop nephritic syndrome, leading to edema and sometimes gross hematuria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute tubular necrosis is not the renal manifestation described for GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nephrotic syndrome is named among the variable renal manifestations of Henoch-Schonlein purpura; the renal lesion described for GPA is nephritic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Obstructive uropathy is not part of the small-vessel vasculitis of GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal papillary necrosis is not a feature of GPA.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl develops purpuric lesions on her buttocks and legs, arthralgias, colicky abdominal pain with intestinal bleeding, and microscopic hematuria. Her disease shares its basic immunologic mechanism, immune-complex deposition, with which of the following?

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura, like SLE, is caused by immune-complex deposition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Henoch-Schonlein purpura occurs in childhood with purpuric skin lesions, abdominal pain and intestinal bleeding, arthralgias, and renal abnormalities. Similar to SLE, HSP is due to immune complex deposition, usually with IgA with or without IgG and complement (C3); SLE is likewise a type 3 hypersensitivity reaction with immune-complex deposition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by circulating autoantibodies binding type IV collagen in basement membranes, not by deposition of immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is caused by PR3-ANCAs that activate neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple sclerosis is an organ-specific autoimmune disease targeting myelin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 1 diabetes is an organ-specific autoimmune attack on pancreatic beta cells.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with palpable purpura on the extensor surfaces of his legs and buttocks develops gross hematuria. Renal biopsy with a Jones stain shows an adhesion to Bowman capsule, early crescent formation, and an increase in mesangial matrix. Immunofluorescence is most likely to show which of the following?

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgM rheumatoid factor in the mesangium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linear IgG along the basement membrane

explanation.summary: Renal involvement in Henoch-Schonlein purpura shows global and diffuse mesangial deposition of IgA on immunofluorescence.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Henoch-Schonlein purpura the kidney may show an adhesion to Bowman capsule, early crescent formation, and increased mesangial matrix on Jones stain, and immunofluorescence shows global and diffuse mesangial deposition of IgA. Renal manifestations range from gross or microscopic hematuria to nephrotic or nephritic syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSP is an immune-complex disease with IgA and complement deposition, so deposits are present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies characterize granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not HSP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatoid factor is an IgM autoantibody of rheumatoid arthritis and is not the glomerular deposit of HSP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Linear IgG along the basement membrane is the pattern of anti-type IV collagen antibody in Goodpasture syndrome.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with fatigue, arthralgias, and a photosensitive facial rash. Her physician suspects a systemic autoimmune disease and plans serologic testing. Which of the following tests is usually the initial step in the laboratory work-up?

explanation.summary: An ANA test is usually the initial step in the serologic work-up of suspected autoimmune disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune diseases are diagnosed with a combination of clinical picture and autoantibody testing. A test for ANAs is usually the initial step in a work-up; if it is positive, sub-serologies such as anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, anti-scl-70, anti-centromere, anti-histone, and anti-Jo are then done to determine the type of ANA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere is one of the sub-serologies checked after a positive ANA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-dsDNA is a sub-serology used to confirm SLE once the ANA is positive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-histone is a sub-serology, not the usual first test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-Smith is a sub-serology performed after a positive ANA, not the initial screen.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a flare of systemic lupus erythematosus is started on high-dose prednisone. Which of the following best describes how corticosteroids act in the treatment of autoimmune disease?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bind proteinase 3 within the granules of neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonspecifically block the normal immune response

choices.label: D
choices.text: Remove circulating autoantibodies from the plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selectively neutralize circulating IgA immune complexes

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids are nonspecific immunomodulators that block the normal immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The basic principle behind treating autoimmune diseases is immunosuppression. Corticosteroids and monoclonal antibodies are the two main medications of choice; corticosteroids are nonspecific immunomodulators that block the normal immune response, whereas monoclonal antibodies bind specific immune modulators.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding TNF-alpha is the mechanism of monoclonal antibody TNF-alpha inhibitors such as infliximab, not corticosteroids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids do not target proteinase 3; PR3 is the antigen of ANCA in granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removal of antibodies from plasma is plasmapheresis, used in Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corticosteroids act nonspecifically rather than neutralizing a particular immune complex.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded adequately to initial therapy is started on adalimumab. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds the Fc portion of IgG

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocks the CD4 coreceptor on helper T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removes immune complexes from the plasma

explanation.summary: Adalimumab is a monoclonal antibody TNF-alpha inhibitor that binds TNF-alpha to suppress the immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monoclonal antibodies bind to specific immune modulators, inhibiting their normal function of inciting components of the inflammatory response. One example is a TNF-alpha inhibitor such as infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab, or golimumab; these function by binding TNF-alpha, a marker released during inflammation, which acts to suppress the immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding the Fc portion of IgG describes rheumatoid factor, an autoantibody, not a therapeutic monoclonal antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TNF-alpha inhibitors bind a cytokine, not the CD4 molecule on helper T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B-cell depletion is not the mechanism of the TNF-alpha inhibitors named.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Removal of material from plasma is plasmapheresis, not the action of adalimumab.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman develops episodes of visual loss and limb weakness that resolve and recur, and she is diagnosed with an autoimmune disease directed against myelin in the central nervous system. Which of the following best classifies her disease?

explanation.summary: Multiple sclerosis, which targets central nervous system myelin, is an organ-specific autoimmune disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In some autoimmune diseases the immune response is directed against a single organ or tissue, resulting in organ-specific disease. Examples include type 1 diabetes mellitus (beta cells), multiple sclerosis (myelin in the central nervous system), and autoimmune hepatitis (liver cells), in contrast to systemic diseases like SLE and rheumatoid arthritis that affect multiple organ systems.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity, unrelated to autoimmune demyelination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune-complex deposition is the mechanism of SLE and Henoch-Schonlein purpura, not the defining feature of an attack on myelin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small-vessel vasculitis describes granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not a disease targeting myelin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Systemic autoimmune diseases such as SLE affect multiple organ systems; an attack confined to central nervous system myelin is organ-specific.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl develops fever, swollen and painful knees and ankles, and a new heart murmur approximately 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat. A throat culture obtained at the earlier visit had grown gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of her current cardiac and joint findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-reacting with host antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of preformed bacterial enterotoxin directly within the affected tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct bacterial seeding and invasion of the myocardium and synovium

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation releasing vasoactive mediators

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superantigen-mediated massive cytokine release causing refractory shock

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is an antibody-mediated autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis driven by molecular mimicry.
explanation.whyCorrect: In group A streptococcal infection the M protein is structurally similar to host antigens, so antibodies generated against it cross-react with self-antigens in the heart, joints, skin, and brain. This molecular mimicry produces acute rheumatic fever roughly 2 weeks after the initiating pharyngitis, injuring tissues that were never directly infected.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterotoxin-mediated disease (e.g., toxic shock) is a direct toxin effect and does not explain antibody cross-reactivity weeks later.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rheumatic fever damages uninfected tissues through the immune response, not by direct bacterial invasion of the heart or joints.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is not the mechanism of rheumatic fever, which is antibody cross-reaction against self-antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superantigen-driven cytokine release produces toxic shock, not the delayed autoimmune carditis and arthritis seen here.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a childhood history of rheumatic fever is found to have a mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex. Echocardiography demonstrates a thickened mitral valve with fused chordae tendineae. Which of the following long-term valvular consequences is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Chronic rheumatic heart disease scars the mitral valve, producing mitral stenosis as an important long-term consequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: In rheumatic heart disease the acute endocardial inflammation and vegetations (verrucae) evolve over time into fibrosis, diffuse thickening of the valve leaflets, and fusion of the tendinous cords. This scarring narrows the mitral orifice, and mitral stenosis is described as an important long-term consequence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitral valve prolapse results from myxomatous degeneration of the leaflets and produces a mid-systolic click, not the mid-diastolic murmur of rheumatic scarring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An atrial septal defect is a congenital shunt, not a result of chronic rheumatic leaflet and chordae scarring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tricuspid atresia is a congenital malformation, not an acquired consequence of rheumatic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A ventricular septal defect is a congenital septal lesion unrelated to rheumatic valve damage.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops dark, cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and elevated blood pressure 2 weeks after a honey-crusted skin infection. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria, and BUN and serum creatinine are elevated. Electron microscopy of a renal biopsy would most likely reveal which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Foot process effacement without immune deposits

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splitting and lamellation of the glomerular basement membrane

explanation.summary: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-complex disease that produces subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a group A strep infection such as impetigo, scarlet fever, or pharyngitis and results from deposition of immune complexes (streptococcal antigen, antibody, and complement) in the glomeruli. Electron microscopy shows subepithelial 'humps' representing these antigen-antibody complexes, and immunofluorescence highlights granular IgG and C3 deposits.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Foot process effacement without deposits describes minimal change disease, which is not post-infectious.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Linear IgG along the basement membrane is characteristic of anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, not immune-complex PSGN.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions are a feature of diabetic nephropathy, unrelated to a preceding streptococcal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Basement membrane splitting is seen in hereditary Alport syndrome, not in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy who recently recovered from streptococcal pharyngitis develops involuntary, dance-like movements of the limbs and darting movements of the tongue. Antibodies in this condition are most likely directed against which of the following structures?

explanation.summary: Sydenham chorea results from an autoimmune attack on the basal ganglia after group A streptococcal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: An autoimmune response against antigens in the basal ganglia produces the subsequent inflammation of Sydenham chorea, classically described as involuntary dance-like movements of the limbs and dart-like movements of the tongue. It is a neurologic consequence of acute rheumatic fever and traditionally resolves over weeks to months.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies against cardiac antigens produce rheumatic carditis, not the movement disorder described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal injury in the post-streptococcal setting is due to immune-complex deposition, not antibodies targeting the movement centers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral nerve myelin is not the described target; chorea reflects central basal ganglia involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, which is unrelated to post-streptococcal chorea.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops conjunctivitis, urethritis, and asymmetric arthritis of the knees several weeks after a diarrheal illness. Arthrocentesis yields sterile synovial fluid, and he is HLA-B27 positive. Which of the following best explains why his arthritis is not expected to respond to antibiotics?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The arthritis is caused by urate crystal deposition

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bacteria have formed a protective biofilm within the joint

choices.label: D
choices.text: The causative bacteria are inherently resistant to all antibiotics

choices.label: E
choices.text: The joint inflammation is an immune response to the earlier infection

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis is an immune-mediated, sterile joint inflammation triggered by a prior infection, so antibiotics do not treat the joint disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactive arthritis is a classic triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis that follows genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. The joint pain is not caused by the infection itself but by an immune response to it, possibly via molecular mimicry, and it is associated with HLA-B27; because the joint is sterile, antibiotics do not resolve the arthritis, which typically resolves within about 6 months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotic penetration is not the issue because there are no organisms in the joint to eradicate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crystal deposition causes gout or pseudogout, not the post-infectious triad described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no live biofilm in the joint; the synovial fluid is sterile in reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The organisms are not uniquely pan-resistant; the joint simply is not infected, so antibiotics have no target there.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with fever and a warm, swollen, painful right knee. Arthrocentesis yields purulent fluid, and Gram stain reveals gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following best characterizes this arthritis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive arthritis due to molecular mimicry

explanation.summary: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes an infectious (septic) arthritis in which organisms can be recovered from the joint fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: In contrast to Chlamydia, which triggers a reactive arthritis, N. gonorrhoeae causes an infectious (septic) arthritis, and the bacteria can be isolated directly from the synovial fluid. Finding gram-negative diplococci in purulent joint fluid confirms organisms are present within the joint.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crystal-induced arthritis shows crystals, not gram-negative diplococci, in the joint aspirate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatous vasculitis is a feature of GPA, not an acute purulent gonococcal joint infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive arthritis (from Chlamydia or enteric bacteria) produces a sterile joint, whereas here diplococci are seen in the fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A sterile immune-complex arthritis would not show organisms on Gram stain of the synovial fluid.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: Two gram-negative diplococci are compared. One frequently remains localized to the genital mucosa, whereas the other readily enters the bloodstream from the nasopharynx to cause meningitis and a vasculitic skin rash. Which feature best explains the disseminating organism's ability to evade phagocytosis and spread?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Production of streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B

explanation.summary: Neisseria meningitidis has a polysaccharide capsule that helps it escape phagocytosis and disseminate, unlike N. gonorrhoeae.
explanation.whyCorrect: In contrast to N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis possesses a polysaccharide capsule that aids in escaping phagocytosis, so it can more readily enter the bloodstream and spread throughout the body, causing purulent meningitis, vasculitic rash, and pyogenic arthritis. N. gonorrhoeae lacks this capsule and therefore usually remains localized.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inability to synthesize ATP describes Chlamydia trachomatis, not the disseminating Neisseria species.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M protein is a group A streptococcal surface protein, not a feature of Neisseria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracytoplasmic inclusions are a feature of Chlamydia trachomatis, not of encapsulated meningococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyogenic exotoxin B (SPEB) is a streptococcal antigen involved in PSGN, not a Neisseria virulence factor.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has mucopurulent cervicitis. The causative organism is a gram-negative bacterium that forms intracytoplasmic inclusions and cannot be grown on standard cell-free media. Which of the following best explains why this organism must live inside host cells?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depends on host enzymes to produce its capsule

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an obligate anaerobe killed by oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks a cell wall entirely

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires host antibodies for replication

explanation.summary: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen because it cannot make its own ATP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia trachomatis is a gram-negative bacterium that cannot synthesize ATP, an essential energy molecule, so it must live inside cells as an obligate intracellular pathogen. As part of its developmental cycle it forms intracytoplasmic inclusions, and it commonly causes lower genital tract infections such as urethritis and mucopurulent cervicitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Its intracellular lifestyle is due to lack of ATP synthesis, not a need for host enzymes to build a capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chlamydia is not described as an obligate anaerobe; its intracellular niche relates to energy dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chlamydia does have a cell wall; its intracellular dependence stems from its inability to generate ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Host antibodies are part of the immune defense and are not required for chlamydial replication.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 32-year-old African-American woman presents with several months of dry cough and dyspnea. Chest imaging shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and biopsy of a lymph node reveals non-necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated giant cells; special stains and cultures for organisms are negative. Which laboratory finding would most support the suspected diagnosis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated serum anti-streptolysin O antibody titer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive acid-fast bacilli stain on biopsy

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis is a non-necrotizing granulomatous disease supported by an elevated serum ACE level.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown etiology that classically affects young adults with a higher incidence in women and African-American patients, presenting with cough, dyspnea, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with non-necrotizing granulomas. Because it is a diagnosis of exclusion, an elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is a helpful supportive laboratory finding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An elevated anti-streptolysin O titer indicates a preceding streptococcal infection, not sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A positive acid-fast bacilli stain indicates mycobacterial infection and would exclude sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PR3-ANCA points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which features necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis, not the sarcoid picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-B27 is associated with reactive arthritis and spondyloarthropathies, not with sarcoidosis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A patient with pulmonary granulomas is being evaluated for possible sarcoidosis. Which of the following findings would be INCOMPATIBLE with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis?

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion, so evidence of an infectious cause such as a positive AFB stain is incompatible with it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagnosis of sarcoidosis is one of exclusion, meaning every other possibility for the granulomatous inflammation, especially infectious etiologies, must be excluded. A positive acid-fast bacilli stain indicates mycobacterial infection and would preclude a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An elevated serum ACE level supports, rather than excludes, a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythema nodosum is a recognized skin manifestation of sarcoidosis and does not exclude it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multinucleated giant cells are a typical component of sarcoid granulomas and are compatible with the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Non-necrotizing granulomas are the classic and expected histology of sarcoidosis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with chronic sinusitis and epistaxis, hemoptysis with nodular lung lesions, and a rapidly rising serum creatinine with hematuria. Biopsy shows necrotizing granulomas of the respiratory tract and small-vessel vasculitis. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be positive?

explanation.summary: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis mediated by anti-proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA).
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is characterized by the clinical triad of acute necrotizing granulomas of the respiratory tract, granulomatous vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. It is an autoimmune disease mediated by anti-proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA, previously c-ANCA).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited scleroderma (CREST), not GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-double-stranded DNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, not GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-GBM antibodies cause Goodpasture syndrome, which lacks the necrotizing respiratory granulomas of GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-streptolysin O reflects prior streptococcal infection and is unrelated to granulomatous vasculitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A skin biopsy demonstrates epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells surrounding flake-like material that is refractile and appears bright under polarized light. This finding is most consistent with which of the following clinical histories?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tick bite transmitting a spirochete

choices.label: D
choices.text: Injection of drugs contaminated with talc

explanation.summary: A foreign body granuloma with birefringent flake-like material and giant cells is characteristic of injected talc from IV drug use.
explanation.whyCorrect: Foreign body granulomas form around non-digestible material and are identified histologically by histiocytic inflammation with epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells surrounding the material without a T-cell-mediated response. Inhaled or injected drugs such as heroin or cocaine can introduce talc into the tissue, and under polarized light the birefringent talc appears bright, exactly as described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlamydia infection is associated with reactive arthritis and cervicitis, not a foreign body granulomatous reaction to injected material.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A spirochetal infection can cause a necrotizing infectious granuloma but would not produce birefringent flake-like foreign material.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The described flake-like birefringent material surrounded by giant cells fits injected talc, not the pleural disease produced by asbestos.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis leads to immune-mediated sequelae such as rheumatic fever and PSGN, not a birefringent foreign body granuloma.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with fever, hypotension, a diffuse erythematous rash, and evidence of liver, kidney, and coagulation dysfunction that developed over the past day. Cultures grow a toxin-producing gram-positive coccus. Which of the following best explains the multi-system organ disease in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A superantigen triggering a massive release of cytokines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies against a bacterial surface protein cross-reacting with host tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacterial dissemination aided by a polysaccharide capsule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes in small vessels

explanation.summary: Superantigen toxins cause immune-mediated collateral damage by triggering a massive cytokine release that can produce hypotension and multi-system organ disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infectious agents damage the host directly, but the immune response to infection also inflicts collateral damage on uninfected tissues. Superantigen toxins are one such mechanism: they trigger a massive release of cytokines, which can result in hypotension and multi-system organ disease, matching this patient's acute shock-like presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody cross-reactivity (molecular mimicry) produces delayed autoimmune disease such as acute rheumatic fever, not acute cytokine-driven shock within a day.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A polysaccharide capsule helps N. meningitidis escape phagocytosis and disseminate; it is not the mechanism of toxin-driven cytokine release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition underlies poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and develops weeks after infection rather than causing acute hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Granulomatous inflammation is a chronic process that damages tissue and heals with scarring; it does not produce acute shock.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy develops fever, migrating joint pain, and a new murmur. His mother recalls that he had a sore throat about 3 weeks earlier that was not treated. Which of the following best explains why his current illness did not appear until several weeks after the throat infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial toxin had to accumulate in the heart and joints over time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement levels had to be depleted before tissue injury could begin

choices.label: C
choices.text: The adaptive immune system needed time to generate the pathogenic antibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bacteria remained latent in the pharynx before reactivating

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism required weeks to spread hematogenously to the heart

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is antibody-mediated, so its onset is delayed about 2 weeks or longer while the adaptive immune system generates the cross-reactive antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute rheumatic fever is the potential autoimmune reaction following a group A streptococcal infection and typically occurs in pediatric patients 5 to 15 years of age. Because it is an antibody-mediated disease and antibodies must be generated by the adaptive immune system, onset occurs approximately 2 weeks or longer after the initial GAS infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The injury is not a direct toxin effect; it is produced by immunoglobulins directed at the M protein that recognize self-antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement is activated during the autoimmune attack on the heart, but complement depletion is not the reason for the delayed onset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatic fever is not caused by bacterial latency and reactivation; it results from antibodies that cross-react with host tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The heart and joints are not infected in rheumatic fever; the damage is an autoimmune attack on uninfected tissue.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for possible acute rheumatic fever 3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis using the Jones Criteria. Which of the following findings is one of the major criteria?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Punctate rash with a sandpaper-like feel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tender red nodules of the lower extremities

explanation.summary: The major Jones Criteria for acute rheumatic fever are carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Jones Criteria are used for diagnosing acute rheumatic fever and rely on major and minor criteria for low-risk and moderate-to-high-risk populations. The major criteria include carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules; subcutaneous nodules occur secondary to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction with a granulomatous response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematuria and proteinuria are features of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, a separate immune-complex consequence of GAS infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Honey-colored crusts describe impetigo, a bacterial skin infection, not a criterion for rheumatic fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A punctate sandpaper-like rash is scarlet fever, caused by streptococcal pyogenic exotoxins, and is not a major criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tender red nodules of the lower extremities describe erythema nodosum, a nonspecific finding associated with sarcoidosis, not a Jones criterion.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy dies during an episode of acute rheumatic fever. Microscopic examination of the heart shows nodules composed of lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and activated macrophages. Which of the following terms best describes these nodules?

explanation.summary: Aschoff bodies are the microscopic nodules of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and activated macrophages seen in the acute phase of rheumatic heart disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In rheumatic heart disease, antibodies against streptococcal M protein recognize cardiac antigens, leading to complement activation, recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages, and cytokine production. In the acute phase, Aschoff bodies, microscopic nodules of lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and activated macrophages, are seen and are a classic finding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Asteroid bodies are star-shaped inclusions in histiocytes that may be seen in sarcoidosis, not in rheumatic carditis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foreign body granulomas form around indigestible material such as sutures or talc and are not a feature of rheumatic carditis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Subepithelial humps are electron-microscopic immune-complex deposits in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, not cardiac lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Verrucae are the gross endocardial vegetations formed from accumulated necrotic debris, not microscopic inflammatory nodules.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl with fever, polyarthritis, and a heart murmur 3 weeks after untreated pharyngitis develops a red, serpiginous, non-pruritic rash on her trunk. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this rash?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the epidermis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in dermal vessels

explanation.summary: Erythema marginatum in acute rheumatic fever is thought to result from antibody cross-reaction (molecular mimicry) to keratin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema marginatum manifests as a red, serpiginous skin lesion in the context of acute rheumatic fever. It is thought to be caused by antibody cross-reaction to keratin, one of the self-antigens recognized by immunoglobulins directed at the streptococcal M protein.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A delayed hypersensitivity reaction with a granulomatous response produces the subcutaneous nodules of rheumatic fever, not the rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rheumatic fever injures uninfected tissues through the immune response; the skin is not directly invaded by bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition is the mechanism of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and of the synovial inflammation in rheumatic arthritis, not of erythema marginatum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcal pyogenic exotoxins cause the punctate, sandpaper-like rash of scarlet fever, not the serpiginous rash of rheumatic fever.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with acute rheumatic fever develops firm, painless nodules beneath the skin over the extensor surfaces of his elbows. Which of the following immune mechanisms is most likely responsible for these nodules?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Foreign body reaction to indigestible material

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the dermis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune complexes binding within the dermis

explanation.summary: Subcutaneous nodules in acute rheumatic fever occur secondary to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction with a granulomatous response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the skin manifestations of acute rheumatic fever, erythema marginatum results from antibody cross-reaction to keratin, whereas subcutaneous nodules may occur secondary to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction with a granulomatous response. Subcutaneous nodules are one of the major Jones Criteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody cross-reaction with keratin produces erythema marginatum, the serpiginous rash, rather than the nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A foreign body reaction to talc occurs with injected or inhaled drugs and is unrelated to poststreptococcal autoimmunity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is a type I hypersensitivity mechanism and is not described in the pathogenesis of rheumatic fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune complexes binding within the synovial membranes explain the migrating polyarthritis of rheumatic fever, not the subcutaneous nodules.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with acute rheumatic fever reports that her right knee was swollen and painful 2 days ago, but today the knee feels better while her left ankle and right wrist have become painful and swollen. Which of the following best explains this joint involvement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune attack against the basal ganglia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct streptococcal infection of the synovial fluid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complexes binding within the synovial membranes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urate crystal deposition in the joint space

explanation.summary: The migrating polyarthritis of acute rheumatic fever is thought to result from immune complexes that bind within joints such as the synovial membranes.
explanation.whyCorrect: In acute rheumatic fever, the immune response creates immune complexes that bind within joints, such as the synovial membranes, leading to increasing inflammation. This is thought to be responsible for the migrating polyarthritis, in which pain 'moves' between different joints, exactly as this patient describes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An autoimmune response against the basal ganglia produces Sydenham chorea, the neurologic manifestation, not arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rheumatic fever damages uninfected tissue through the immune response; the joints are not directly infected by streptococci.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactive arthritis follows genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections and is associated with HLA-B27; it is not the arthritis of rheumatic fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urate crystal deposition causes gout, which is not a poststreptococcal phenomenon and does not explain migrating polyarthritis in a child.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl presents with involuntary, dance-like movements of the limbs and darting movements of the tongue that began after a throat infection almost 2 months ago. Her father is worried the condition will be permanent. Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding the expected course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The movements are permanent because basal ganglia neurons have been destroyed

choices.label: B
choices.text: The movements usually resolve within weeks to months without treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: The movements will progress to seizures and cognitive decline

choices.label: D
choices.text: The movements will recur every time she has a viral illness

choices.label: E
choices.text: The movements will resolve only after several months of antibiotics

explanation.summary: Sydenham chorea is traditionally believed to resolve without treatment within weeks to months, although long-term neurologic consequences have been reported.
explanation.whyCorrect: This girl has rheumatic (Sydenham) chorea, caused by molecular mimicry in which antibodies generated against GAS M protein cross-react with the basal ganglia. Traditionally, it is believed that Sydenham chorea resolves without treatment within weeks to months, but long-term neurologic consequences are reported, so the parent should be told it is usually self-limiting although some patients have longer-term consequences.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sydenham chorea is traditionally considered self-limiting rather than permanent, so stating it is irreversible is inaccurate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seizures and cognitive changes are nervous system manifestations of sarcoidosis, not the expected course of Sydenham chorea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrence with every viral illness is not a described feature of Sydenham chorea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The chorea is an autoimmune phenomenon that traditionally resolves without treatment; antibiotics are not what resolves the movement disorder.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with a sore throat and fever develops a diffuse, punctate, erythematous rash that is accentuated over the trunk and inner aspects of the limbs and feels like sandpaper. Which of the following is the cause of this rash?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in dermal vessels

explanation.summary: Scarlet fever is a pediatric streptococcal infection whose punctate, sandpaper-like rash is caused by streptococcal pyogenic exotoxins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Scarlet fever is the term for a pediatric streptococcal infection, usually of the throat, accompanied by a characteristic punctate, erythematous rash typically accentuated over the trunk and inner aspects of the limbs. The minute papules give the rash a sandpaper-like feel, and the rash is caused by streptococcal pyogenic exotoxins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody cross-reaction with keratin causes erythema marginatum, a serpiginous rash of acute rheumatic fever, not the punctate rash of scarlet fever.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delayed hypersensitivity with a granulomatous response produces the subcutaneous nodules of rheumatic fever, not scarlet fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune complex deposition explains poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows scarlet fever weeks later, rather than the rash itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A vasculitic rash from an encapsulated organism describes disseminated N. meningitidis infection, not scarlet fever.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is found to have a blood pressure of 142/94 mm Hg, periorbital edema, and cola-colored urine 2 weeks after an episode of scarlet fever. Which of the following best explains his elevated blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody cross-reaction with vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune attack on the basal ganglia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired fluid and sodium maintenance by injured glomeruli

choices.label: E
choices.text: Massive cytokine release triggered by a superantigen

explanation.summary: Hypertension in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a consequence of impaired fluid and sodium maintenance by the injured filtering units of the kidney.
explanation.whyCorrect: In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, immune complexes of streptococcal antigens, antibodies, and complement deposit in renal glomeruli and injure the filtering units of the kidneys. The resulting clinical features include hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension as a consequence of impaired fluid and sodium maintenance, and azotemia from impaired removal of BUN and creatinine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody cross-reaction underlies rheumatic fever; PSGN is caused by immune complex deposition, not antibodies against vessel walls.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An autoimmune attack on the basal ganglia produces Sydenham chorea and does not explain hypertension or renal findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomatous vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels is a feature of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not poststreptococcal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superantigen-triggered cytokine release causes hypotension and shock, the opposite of this patient's hypertension.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with cough, dyspnea, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy develops several tender, red nodules on the anterior and lateral surfaces of both lower legs. Which of the following terms best describes these skin lesions?

explanation.summary: Erythema nodosum refers to tender, red nodules most commonly found on the anterior and lateral lower extremities and is a nonspecific finding that may represent skin involvement by sarcoidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Skin manifestations of sarcoidosis include erythema nodosum, maculopapular lesions, and lupus pernio. Erythema nodosum is a nonspecific finding consisting of red, tender nodules most commonly found on the anterior and lateral lower extremities, matching this patient with respiratory symptoms and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythema marginatum is a red, serpiginous lesion seen in acute rheumatic fever, not tender nodules of the legs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impetigo is a bacterial skin infection with honey-colored crusts and superficial erosions, typically of the face.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lupus pernio is a pattern of painful lesions of the nose, beneath the eyes, and cheeks in sarcoidosis, not lower-extremity nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subcutaneous nodules in rheumatic fever are firm nodules from a granulomatous delayed hypersensitivity reaction, not tender red leg nodules in a sarcoidosis patient.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man develops painful swelling of the left knee, burning with urination, and red eyes 3 weeks after an episode of bloody diarrhea. Synovial fluid is sterile. Which of the following organisms most likely triggered his current condition?

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis may follow gastrointestinal infections with Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, or Yersinia, as well as genitourinary infection with Chlamydia trachomatis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactive arthritis is a classic triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis that may occur secondary to genitourinary infections such as C. trachomatis or after gastrointestinal infections including Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, and Yersinia. Symptoms typically develop within days or weeks of the initiating infection, and the sterile joint fluid confirms an immune-mediated rather than infectious arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histoplasma capsulatum is a fungus that causes necrotizing granulomatous infection and is not a described trigger of reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: N. gonorrhoeae causes an infectious (septic) arthritis in which bacteria can be isolated from synovial fluid, and it is not a gastrointestinal trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: N. meningitidis causes meningitis, vasculitic rash, and pyogenic arthritis after nasopharyngeal carriage, not post-diarrheal reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes leads to acute rheumatic fever or poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after pharyngitis or skin infection, not reactive arthritis after diarrhea.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with reactive arthritis following a Chlamydia trachomatis infection tests positive for HLA-B27. Which of the following best describes HLA-B27?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polysaccharide capsule antigen of Neisseria

choices.label: B
choices.text: A streptococcal surface antigen that resists phagocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: A subtype of class I major histocompatibility complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: A subtype of class II major histocompatibility complex

explanation.summary: HLA-B27 is a subtype of class I MHC that confers increased risk for reactive arthritis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactive arthritis is strongly associated with the HLA-B27 phenotype. HLA-B27 is a subtype of the class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC-I), and its presence confers increased risk for reactive arthritis as well as ankylosing spondylitis and inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The polysaccharide capsule is a feature of N. meningitidis that aids escape from phagocytosis; HLA-B27 is a human MHC molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The streptococcal surface antigen that resists phagocytosis is the M protein, a bacterial virulence factor rather than a host molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-B27 belongs to class I, not class II, of the major histocompatibility complex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA) is the autoantibody mediating granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not a histocompatibility antigen.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with no complaints undergoes routine screening and is found to have a lower genital tract infection with a gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium. Which of the following features of this organism most contributes to its spread in the population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polysaccharide capsule allows escape from phagocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Asymptomatic carriage in the nasopharynx with droplet spread

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression of an antiphagocytic M protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many infected men and women remain asymptomatic

explanation.summary: Chlamydia trachomatis infections are frequently asymptomatic in both men and women, which contributes to the spread of the organism.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. trachomatis is a common sexually transmitted infection responsible for lower genital tract infections including urethritis and mucopurulent cervicitis. Many men and women remain asymptomatic, a fact that contributes to the spread of the organism, which is why screening identifies infections like this one.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A polysaccharide capsule is the feature of N. meningitidis that allows dissemination; it is not described for Chlamydia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nasopharyngeal carriage with respiratory droplet spread describes N. meningitidis transmission, not a sexually transmitted genital infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M protein is the antiphagocytic surface protein of group A streptococcus, not of Chlamydia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superantigen toxins produce cytokine-driven shock and are not a feature of C. trachomatis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 6-day-old girl born vaginally develops bilateral eyelid swelling with mucoid discharge. Her mother had no prenatal care. Which of the following measures would most likely have prevented this infant's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isolation of the newborn from respiratory droplet exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Screening of the mother for sexually transmitted genital infections

choices.label: C
choices.text: Testing of the mother for the HLA-B27 phenotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Treatment of the mother for group A streptococcal pharyngitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaccination of the mother against Neisseria meningitidis before delivery

explanation.summary: Both C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae can be transmitted through the birth canal to cause neonatal conjunctivitis, so maternal screening is important for prevention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae can be transmitted to the neonate through the birth canal, resulting in neonatal conjunctivitis with eyelid swelling and mucoid discharge. Maternal screening is important to preventing these infections, and this mother's lack of prenatal care meant she was never screened.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neonatal conjunctivitis from these organisms is acquired during passage through the birth canal, not from respiratory droplets after birth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-B27 is associated with reactive arthritis and has no role in preventing vertical transmission of genital pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptococcal pharyngitis leads to rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis in the infected child, not to neonatal conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: N. meningitidis vaccination prevents meningococcal disease in enclosed communities; it does not prevent vertically transmitted conjunctivitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: Gram-negative diplococci recovered from a urethral swab are studied for their ability to invade epithelial cells. The long pili on the surface of this organism bind to which of the following host molecules?

explanation.summary: Neisseria species invade epithelial cells using long pili that bind CD46 on human cells, with OPA proteins facilitating entry.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neisseria spp. are gram-negative diplococci and intracellular pathogens. They invade epithelial cells using long pili, which bind to CD46, a protein on human cells, and OPA ('opacity') proteins then facilitate entry into the epithelial cells, where the organisms replicate before extracellular release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is elevated in the serum of sarcoidosis patients; it is not a bacterial attachment site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-B27 is a class I MHC subtype associated with reactive arthritis; it is not the ligand for Neisseria pili.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratin is the self-antigen targeted by cross-reactive antibodies in erythema marginatum, not a Neisseria receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Proteinase 3 is the target of PR3-ANCA in granulomatosis with polyangiitis and is unrelated to Neisseria adhesion.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents with fever, a painful swollen right knee that yields purulent fluid, and painful, erythematous, hemorrhagic pustules on her palms, fingers, and extensor elbows. She has no headache or nuchal rigidity, and a cervical swab grows gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Rare disseminated gonococcal infection presents with skin rash, purulent arthritis, and fever after gonococcal bacteremia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gonococcal infections tend to be localized, but in rare instances they disseminate through gonococcal bacteremia, manifesting with skin rash, purulent arthritis, and fever. The rash consists of painful, erythematous, hemorrhagic pustules on the palms, fingers, and extensor elbows, and biopsy shows vasculitis and thrombosis with diplococci visible on tissue Gram stain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute rheumatic fever causes migrating polyarthritis with sterile joints weeks after pharyngitis and does not produce hemorrhagic pustules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactive arthritis produces sterile joint fluid with urethritis and conjunctivitis; purulent arthritis with organisms indicates septic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sarcoidosis causes non-necrotizing granulomas, hilar lymphadenopathy, and erythema nodosum, not an acute febrile pustular illness with purulent arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scarlet fever is a pediatric streptococcal throat infection with a punctate sandpaper rash, not hemorrhagic pustules and purulent arthritis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: An 18-year-old college freshman living in a dormitory develops fever, headache, a stiff neck, and a petechial rash; gram-negative diplococci are identified in cerebrospinal fluid. Which of the following would most likely have prevented this illness?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Treatment of an earlier streptococcal pharyngitis

explanation.summary: Vaccines against N. meningitidis prevent serious disease and are required by some states for entrance into colleges, where enclosed communities increase transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: Meningitis caused by N. meningitidis occurs in children and adults, and enclosed communities such as educational institutions and military training camps provide an opportunity for increased transmission. Vaccines against N. meningitidis are available to prevent serious disease and are required by some states for entrance into colleges and universities; nuchal rigidity is a classic sign of the purulent meningitis this organism causes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Maternal screening prevents neonatal conjunctivitis from vertical transmission, not meningococcal meningitis in a young adult.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Screening for sexually transmitted infections targets C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae, which cause genital and neonatal disease rather than meningitis in a dormitory setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-B27 testing relates to reactive arthritis risk and has no role in preventing meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Treating streptococcal pharyngitis addresses rheumatic fever risk; it does not prevent meningococcal disease.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a lung nodule resected. Histology shows a granuloma with central necrosis surrounded by multinucleated giant cells, and special stains reveal Histoplasma capsulatum. Which of the following best explains the central necrosis within this granuloma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of a T cell-mediated immune response

choices.label: C
choices.text: Idiopathic macrophage activation by IL-2 and IFN-gamma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inability of histiocytes to digest inert material

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ongoing immune-mediated attack against the pathogen

explanation.summary: Granulomas of mycobacterial, spirochetal, fungal, and parasitic infections are often necrotizing because of the ongoing immune-mediated attack against the pathogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomas may be seen in mycobacterial, spirochetal, fungal, and parasitic infections, among others. Many of these granulomas are necrotizing due to the ongoing, immune-mediated attack against the pathogen, as illustrated by central necrosis with multinucleated giant cells in a Histoplasma capsulatum infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Foreign body granulomas lack a T cell-mediated response; an infectious granuloma is driven by the immune attack on the organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PR3-ANCA-mediated vasculitis is the mechanism of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, an autoimmune disease rather than a fungal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Idiopathic helper T-cell activation of macrophages via IL-2 and IFN-gamma describes sarcoidosis, which produces non-necrotizing granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histiocytes unable to digest inert material form foreign body granulomas around sutures or talc, not necrotizing infectious granulomas.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 62-year-old asymptomatic woman has a chest CT showing a small calcified lung nodule. Biopsy reveals a fibrosed nodule with an old, hyalinized granuloma and secondary calcification; no organisms or active inflammation are identified. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute necrotizing granuloma of granulomatosis with polyangiitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Foreign body reaction to injected talc

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complex deposition after streptococcal infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reparative fibrosis marking a resolved granulomatous infection

explanation.summary: Fibrosed nodules and old, hyalinized granulomas with secondary calcification are markers of a previously resolved granulomatous infection that healed by reparative fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In granulomatous infections, the affected organ parenchyma may not be able to regenerate even after resolution of the infection, resulting in reparative fibrosis (scarring) to heal. Fibrosed nodules and old, hyalinized granulomas, some with secondary calcification, may be markers of such a resolved infection, consistent with this asymptomatic patient's calcified nodule without organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active sarcoidosis shows non-necrotizing granulomas with ongoing inflammation, typically with hilar lymphadenopathy and symptoms, not a burned-out hyalinized calcified nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GPA produces acute necrotizing granulomas of the respiratory tract with vasculitis, an active process rather than an old healed scar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A talc foreign body granuloma shows birefringent flake-like material surrounded by giant cells, not a calcified hyalinized scar in a patient without drug use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition after streptococcal infection injures the glomeruli, not the lung, and does not form calcified granulomas.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with necrotizing granulomas of the respiratory tract and positive PR3-ANCA develops a rise in serum creatinine from 1.1 to 4.6 mg/dL over ten days. Renal biopsy shows glomeruli with crescents. Which of the following best characterizes this renal lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A foreign body granuloma surrounding indigestible material

choices.label: B
choices.text: A necrotizing granuloma centered on the glomerulus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A non-necrotizing granuloma of the renal interstitium

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis that is not a granuloma

choices.label: E
choices.text: A subepithelial immune complex deposit from streptococcal antigen

explanation.summary: The rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a separate histologic consequence of the disease and is not itself a granuloma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is characterized by the triad of acute necrotizing granulomas of the respiratory tract, granulomatous vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, a severe form of glomerular injury with rapid loss of renal function. Rapidly progressive ('crescenteric') glomerulonephritis is not a granuloma but rather another histologic consequence encountered in GPA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A foreign body granuloma forms around sutures, splinters, or talc and has no relation to the ANCA-mediated glomerular injury of GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The necrotizing granulomas of GPA occur in the respiratory tract; the glomerular crescents are not granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Non-necrotizing granulomas are the hallmark of sarcoidosis, and the crescentic glomerular lesion is not granulomatous at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subepithelial humps of streptococcal antigen-antibody complexes characterize poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, not the crescentic GN of GPA.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is diagnosed with sarcoidosis after lymph node biopsy shows non-necrotizing granulomas and infectious causes are excluded. Which of the following best describes the process by which her granulomas formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies against proteinase 3 injuring small vessel walls

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helper T cells activating macrophages through IL-2 and interferon gamma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histiocytes surrounding material too resistant to be digested

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complexes of antigen, antibody, and complement depositing in tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune-mediated attack against a persisting intracellular pathogen

explanation.summary: In sarcoidosis, helper T cells activate macrophages using cytokines such as IL-2 and IFN-gamma, leading to TNF release and formation of non-necrotizing granulomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Though the exact etiology of sarcoidosis is unknown, granulomas are formed due to the activation of macrophages by helper T cells using cytokines such as IL-2 and interferon gamma (IFN-gamma). This leads to more pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and further recruitment and activation of macrophages and lymphocytes, with the end result being non-necrotizing granulomas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-proteinase 3 antibodies mediate granulomatosis with polyangiitis, an autoimmune vasculitis distinct from sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histiocytes surrounding indigestible material describes a foreign body granuloma, which does not generate a T cell-mediated response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition is the mechanism of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, not of sarcoid granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An immune attack against a persisting pathogen produces necrotizing infectious granulomas; sarcoidosis is idiopathic and requires exclusion of infection.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 38-year-old African-American woman with known sarcoidosis develops painful, violaceous, indurated lesions on her nose, beneath her eyes, and over her cheeks. Which of the following terms best describes this pattern of skin involvement?

explanation.summary: Lupus pernio is the pattern of painful sarcoidosis lesions of the nose, beneath the eyes, and cheeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Signs and symptoms of sarcoidosis are highly variable and depend on which organ is affected.
