EBV affects 90% of people worldwide in their lifetime, with primary infection most often in childhood or young adulthood, and it remains latent in circulating B cells but can become reactivated, especially during times of immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes EBV latency in B cells, not hepatocytes; hepatosplenomegaly is a symptom of mononucleosis, not the site of latency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal tubular cells are not described as a site of EBV latency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sensory ganglia are not the site of EBV latency described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endothelial cells are not described as a reservoir for latent EBV.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man undergoes kidney transplantation. Within minutes of vascular anastomosis, the surgeon notes that the graft becomes mottled, cyanotic, and flaccid. Biopsy shows platelet-fibrin thrombi and severe ischemic injury within glomeruli. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD8+ T-cell-mediated destruction of graft parenchymal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of IgE antibodies on mast cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation causing vessel occlusion

explanation.summary: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours due to pre-formed recipient antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours after transplant when the recipient already has pre-formed antibodies that react against ABO blood group antigens or type I MHC molecules on graft endothelial cells. These antibodies trigger the complement cascade, producing thrombosis, ischemia, and necrosis, which matches the platelet-fibrin thrombi seen on biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD8+ T-cell destruction of graft cells describes acute cellular rejection, which occurs one week to several months later, not within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgE on mast cells mediates type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, allergy), not antibody-mediated graft thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue describes graft-versus-host disease, seen mainly after bone marrow transplant, not immediate kidney graft failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intimal proliferation and vessel occlusion characterize chronic rejection, which develops over months to years.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man received an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for acute leukemia. Two weeks later he develops a maculopapular skin rash and watery diarrhea. Which of the following cells is most directly responsible for his symptoms?

explanation.summary: GVHD is caused by donor T cells that recognize recipient tissue as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: These symptoms are graft-versus-host disease after bone marrow transplant. Bone marrow transplant tissue contains many T cells, and in GVHD the donor's transplanted T cells recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and attack organs such as the skin and gut, producing rash and diarrhea. GVHD is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by donor T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Donor plasma cells produce antibody; GVHD injury results from donor T-cell cytotoxicity and cytokine release, not humoral immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor B cells have not been found to cause the symptoms of GVHD; the reaction is T-cell mediated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recipient natural killer cells are not the described mediator of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recipient T cells drive graft rejection, in which the recipient attacks the graft, the opposite direction of GVHD.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with diabetic nephropathy receives a kidney transplant. Intraoperatively the surgeon notes the organ is pale and poorly perfused; a thrombus has formed and is preventing perfusion of the graft. Which type of rejection is most likely?

explanation.summary: Rejection occurring within minutes of transplantation is hyperacute.
explanation.whyCorrect: The type of rejection described is hyperacute because it occurred within minutes of transplantation, with thrombosis and poor perfusion caused by pre-formed antibodies activating complement on the graft endothelium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute rejection occurs about one week to several months after the transplant, not intraoperatively.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic rejection occurs months to years later and manifests as graft arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Graft-versus-host disease occurs weeks to months after transplant and results mainly from bone marrow transplant, not from an immediate kidney thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subacute rejection is not one of the recognized categories of transplant rejection described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 39-year-old kidney transplant recipient develops rising creatinine 6 weeks after surgery. Biopsy shows inflammatory cells infiltrating between the epithelial cells of the tubules (tubulitis) and CD8+ T cells destroying graft cells. Which of the following best describes this process?

explanation.summary: Tubulitis with CD8+ T-cell-mediated graft cell killing defines acute cellular rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute cellular rejection occurs when CD8+ T cells directly destroy graft cells or CD4+ T cells secrete cytokines and induce inflammation. On kidney biopsy it manifests as tubulitis, with inflammatory cells between the epithelial cells of the tubules, matching this patient's findings weeks after transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies binding endothelium with complement activation and shows C4d deposition and capillaritis, not primarily T-cell tubulitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic rejection develops over months to years with graft arteriosclerosis and fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GVHD involves donor T cells attacking recipient tissue and is characteristic of bone marrow, not kidney, transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours and shows thrombosis, not a T-cell tubulitis weeks later.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old kidney transplant recipient has worsening graft function 2 months post-transplant. Biopsy shows peritubular capillaritis, and an immunoperoxidase stain reveals C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries. Which mechanism is most likely responsible?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct CD8+ T-cell killing of tubular cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor T cells attacking recipient endothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE-mediated release of mast cell mediators

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation occluding vessels

explanation.summary: C4d deposition marks acute antibody-mediated rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: In acute antibody-mediated rejection, antibodies bind to vascular endothelium and activate complement; the resulting inflammation and endothelial damage cause graft failure. The complement split product C4d deposited in peritubular capillaries, demonstrated by immunoperoxidase staining, is the diagnostic marker.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Direct CD8+ T-cell killing describes acute cellular rejection with tubulitis, which is not marked by C4d deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor T cells attacking the recipient describe GVHD, not antibody-mediated rejection of a kidney graft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE and mast cell mediators drive type I hypersensitivity, not complement-fixing antibody rejection of a graft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intimal proliferation with vessel occlusion is a feature of chronic rejection, not C4d-positive antibody-mediated injury.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man who received a heart transplant 4 years ago develops progressive graft dysfunction. Angiography shows diffuse narrowing of the coronary arteries, and biopsy reveals graft arteriosclerosis with intimal smooth muscle proliferation. Which type of rejection does this represent?

explanation.summary: Graft arteriosclerosis developing years after transplant is chronic rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rejection can occur months to years after transplant and involves both cellular and humoral immune responses. It produces graft arteriosclerosis, with intimal smooth muscle proliferation and vessel occlusion, plus interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, matching the coronary narrowing years after a heart transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute antibody-mediated rejection occurs within weeks to months with C4d deposition, not years-long vascular remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute cellular rejection occurs within weeks to months and shows T-cell tubulitis or endothelitis, not chronic arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GVHD is a bone marrow transplant complication in which donor cells attack the recipient, not chronic coronary graft arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours with thrombosis, not slowly progressive arteriosclerosis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops anaphylaxis after a bee sting, with hypotension, urticaria, and bronchospasm. This reaction is mediated by IgE causing release of mast cell mediators. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is this, and which type of transplant rejection shares the antibody-mediated category most analogous to hyperacute rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type I hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type II

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type I hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type IV

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type II hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type I

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type III hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type IV

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type IV hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type III

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is type I; hyperacute rejection is a type II (antibody-mediated) reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type I hypersensitivity is immediate, mediated by IgE antibodies that trigger release of mast cell mediators, producing anaphylaxis, allergies, and bronchial asthma. Hyperacute rejection, caused by pre-formed antibodies activating complement against graft endothelium, is classified as a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anaphylaxis is correctly type I, but hyperacute rejection is type II, not type IV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anaphylaxis is not type II; type II involves IgG/IgM injuring cells, and hyperacute rejection is type II, not type I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anaphylaxis is not type III (immune-complex); hyperacute rejection is not type IV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anaphylaxis is not type IV (T-cell mediated); hyperacute rejection is not type III.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man develops an intensely pruritic, vesicular rash 48 hours after his skin contacts poison ivy. Biopsy shows a T-cell-rich infiltrate with macrophage activation and no antibody deposition. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible?

explanation.summary: Contact dermatitis is a delayed, T-cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type IV hypersensitivity reactions occur when T cells cause either direct cytotoxicity (CD8+ T cells) or induce inflammation and cytokine release (CD4+ T cells) with macrophage activation. Examples include contact dermatitis, type I diabetes, and graft-versus-host disease, consistent with this delayed poison ivy reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I is IgE-mediated and immediate (anaphylaxis, allergy), not a delayed T-cell reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type II involves IgG or IgM injuring cells by phagocytosis or lysis, not T-cell contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type III involves immune-complex deposition (e.g., lupus, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis), not cell-mediated contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type V is not among the four hypersensitivity categories described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A hematologist is counseling a patient before an allogeneic bone marrow transplant about the risk of graft-versus-host disease. Which of the following best explains why GVHD develops in this setting but is rare after solid organ transplants such as kidney?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow transplant tissue contains abundant donor T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor IgE triggers mast cell degranulation in the recipient

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complexes deposit in the recipient's bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recipient CD8+ T cells reject the donor marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: The recipient's pre-formed antibodies react against donor marrow

explanation.summary: GVHD occurs because bone marrow grafts are rich in donor T cells that recognize recipient tissue as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bone marrow transplant tissue typically contains a large number of T cells. Unlike graft rejection, in which the recipient's immune cells recognize the graft as foreign, in GVHD the donor's transplanted T cells recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and attack the recipient's organs, causing severe organ dysfunction. This is why GVHD is characteristic of allogeneic bone marrow, not solid organ, transplants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Donor IgE and mast cells describe type I hypersensitivity, which does not mediate GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune-complex deposition is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism, not the basis of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recipient CD8+ T cells rejecting the graft describes host-versus-graft rejection, the opposite of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pre-formed recipient antibodies against a graft cause hyperacute rejection, not GVHD.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with GVHD after bone marrow transplant develops jaundice with a rising direct bilirubin. Which of the following histopathologic changes best accounts for her jaundice?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patchy epithelial cell death in the epidermis

explanation.summary: Jaundice in GVHD results from immune destruction of small bile ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with GVHD may present with jaundice caused by destruction of the small bile ducts, which impairs bile flow and raises bilirubin. This reflects donor T-cell-mediated attack on recipient hepatic tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Graft arteriosclerosis is a feature of chronic solid-organ rejection, not the cause of GVHD-related jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucosal ulceration of the gut causes the diarrhea of GVHD, not jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Patchy epidermal cell death produces the maculopapular skin rash of GVHD, not jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet-fibrin thrombi characterize hyperacute rejection of a solid organ graft, not GVHD hepatic injury.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is being evaluated for a bone marrow transplant and asks about his risk of graft-versus-host disease. Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for developing GVHD?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complete depletion of donor T cells from the graft

choices.label: E
choices.text: Young donor age with fully matched HLA

explanation.summary: GVHD occurs most frequently in recipients exposed to radiation or with leukemia, autoimmune disease, or immunodeficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: GVHD occurs most frequently in recipients who have been exposed to radiation or who have leukemia, autoimmune diseases, or immunodeficiencies. Other contributing factors include transplantation from female donors to male recipients. Some of this risk relates to immunosuppression of the recipient, reducing the ability to neutralize the donor T-lymphocyte attack.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recipients are typically conditioned with chemotherapy to eradicate marrow; absence of chemotherapy is not a listed GVHD risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GVHD requires an allogeneic (non-identical donor) graft; autologous transplants use the patient's own cells and do not cause GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Depleting donor T cells removes the very cells that mediate GVHD, lowering the risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A young, fully HLA-matched donor reduces rather than increases the alloreactivity that drives GVHD.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A transplant team manages a kidney recipient on multiple immunosuppressive drugs. The team notes that standardized histologic criteria are used to diagnose and grade rejection across organs. Which criteria are used specifically for grading rejection in kidney transplants?

explanation.summary: The Banff criteria are used to grade kidney transplant rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several histologic criteria have been created to diagnose and grade rejection for organ transplants. The Banff criteria are used for kidney transplants, while the ISHLT criteria are applied to heart transplants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Child-Pugh criteria grade chronic liver disease severity, not graft rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ISHLT criteria are used for heart transplant rejection, not kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ranson criteria assess the severity of acute pancreatitis, not transplant rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNM staging describes cancer extent, not transplant rejection grading.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease is evaluated for kidney transplantation. She has had four pregnancies and received multiple blood transfusions during a prior surgery. The transplant team warns that she is at increased risk of hyperacute rejection. Which of the following best explains her elevated risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired IgE sensitization to donor blood group antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic immunosuppression from her prior surgery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of immune complexes in her native kidneys

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expansion of alloreactive CD8+ T cells during pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prior exposure that induced antibodies against MHC molecules

explanation.summary: Prior transfusion, pregnancy, or transplantation can induce anti-MHC antibodies that cause hyperacute rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperacute rejection depends on pre-formed recipient antibodies. Besides natural IgM against blood group antigens, these may be antibodies specific for MHC molecules that were induced by prior exposure to foreign cells through blood transfusion, pregnancy, or transplantation of another organ. Her history of pregnancies and transfusions makes such antibodies likely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection involves IgM or anti-MHC antibodies that activate complement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppression would reduce, not increase, an antibody-mediated response, and surgery does not cause chronic immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune-complex deposition is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism and is not the basis of hyperacute rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperacute rejection is antibody mediated (type 2 hypersensitivity), not driven by CD8+ T cells, which mediate acute cellular rejection.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man undergoes kidney transplantation. Within 30 minutes of reperfusion the graft becomes cyanotic and mottled, and a frozen section shows fibrin-platelet thrombi in glomerular capillaries with ischemic necrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perform a repeat biopsy in 48 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remove the graft as soon as possible

explanation.summary: A hyperacutely rejected graft must be removed as soon as possible.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is hyperacute rejection: pre-formed antibodies against ABO or class I MHC antigens on graft endothelium trigger the complement cascade, producing thrombosis, ischemia, and necrosis within minutes to 24 hours. Because the graft is already irreversibly infarcting, it must be removed as soon as possible.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The process is antibody and complement mediated, not infectious, so antibiotics do not address it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppressive medication treats acute rejection, which responds to it; it cannot reverse complement-mediated thrombosis of an already necrotic graft.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Observation is inappropriate; the graft has undergone ischemic necrosis and requires removal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Waiting 48 hours for another biopsy delays removal of a necrotic organ that cannot be salvaged.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with no history of blood transfusion, prior transplantation, or pregnancy-related exposure receives a kidney from a donor of a different ABO blood group. Minutes after anastomosis the graft thromboses. Which of the following antibodies most likely mediated this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor-derived antibodies against recipient blood group antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgA antibodies deposited in glomerular mesangium

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgE antibodies against donor endothelial proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG antibodies induced against class II MHC molecules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural IgM antibodies against a blood group antigen

explanation.summary: Natural IgM antibodies against ABO blood group antigens cause hyperacute rejection without any prior sensitization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperacute rejection results from pre-formed recipient antibodies that react against ABO blood group antigens or class I MHC molecules on graft endothelial cells. In a patient with no prior sensitizing exposure, the pre-formed antibodies are natural IgM antibodies against a blood group antigen, which exist without prior transfusion, pregnancy, or transplantation and explain the reaction after an ABO-mismatched graft.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperacute rejection is caused by the recipient's antibodies against the graft, not donor antibodies against the recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA mesangial deposition is not the mechanism of graft thrombosis within minutes of transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, allergy), not the complement-fixing type 2 reaction of hyperacute rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-MHC antibodies require induction by prior exposure (transfusion, pregnancy, transplantation), which this patient lacks; the brick names class I MHC, not class II, as the endothelial target.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with hemoptysis and hematuria. Renal biopsy shows IgG antibodies bound along the glomerular basement membrane, and he is diagnosed with Goodpasture syndrome. Which of the following mechanisms of hypersensitivity is responsible for his tissue injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytokine release and macrophage activation driven by CD4+ helper T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of circulating antigen-antibody complexes in tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct cytotoxic killing of target cells by CD8+ T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE-triggered release of mast cell mediators causing vasodilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgG or IgM antibodies injuring cells and inducing inflammation

explanation.summary: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies against cells and tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type II hypersensitivity reactions occur when IgG and IgM antibodies injure cells by promoting their phagocytosis or lysis and induce inflammation. Examples cited include autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Goodpasture syndrome, in which antibody bound to the basement membrane produces the inflammation and injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4+ T-cell cytokine release with macrophage activation is the other arm of type IV hypersensitivity, not an antibody-mediated process.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune-complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, exemplified by lupus and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, not antibody bound directly to tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity is a type IV mechanism seen in contact dermatitis, type I diabetes, and GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE and mast cell mediators characterize type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, allergies, bronchial asthma), not Goodpasture syndrome.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy develops periorbital edema, hypertension, and cola-colored urine 2 weeks after an untreated episode of pharyngitis. He is diagnosed with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of glomerular injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigen-antibody complexes deposited in tissue inducing inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4+ T cells releasing cytokines that activate macrophages in the glomerulus

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells directly killing glomerular epithelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE antibodies bound to mast cells triggering their degranulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgG antibodies bound to glomerular cells promoting their phagocytosis

explanation.summary: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction caused by immune-complex deposition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type III hypersensitivity reactions occur when antigen-antibody complexes (IgG or IgM) are deposited in tissues and induce inflammation and tissue damage. The brick lists lupus and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis as the examples of this mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4+ T-cell cytokine release with macrophage activation is type IV hypersensitivity, exemplified by contact dermatitis and GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity is a type IV mechanism, not the basis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is type I hypersensitivity, seen in anaphylaxis, allergies, and bronchial asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibodies directly injuring cells by promoting phagocytosis or lysis is type II hypersensitivity, as in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Goodpasture syndrome.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with bronchial asthma develops wheezing and chest tightness minutes after exposure to cat dander. Her airway narrowing results from the action of mast cell mediators released in a type I hypersensitivity reaction. On which of the following targets do these mediators act to produce her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood vessels and smooth muscle cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelial cells bearing class I MHC molecules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glomerular basement membrane and tubular epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages and neutrophils in the interstitium

explanation.summary: Type I hypersensitivity mediators act on vessels and smooth muscle, producing vasodilation, edema, smooth muscle contraction, and mucus production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are immediate; IgE antibodies cause release of mast cell mediators, and these mediators act on vessels and smooth muscle cells to produce vasodilation, edema, smooth muscle contraction, and mucus production. Bronchial asthma, anaphylaxis, and allergies are the examples given, and bronchial smooth muscle contraction with mucus production explains her wheezing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Endothelial class I MHC molecules are the target of pre-formed antibodies in hyperacute rejection, a type 2 reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glomerular basement membrane injury is a target of antibody in type II reactions such as Goodpasture syndrome, not of mast cell mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recruitment of macrophages and neutrophils by cytokines is the CD4+ T-cell arm of type IV hypersensitivity and acute cellular rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parenchymal cells bearing alloantigens are killed by CD8+ T cells in acute cellular rejection, not affected by mast cell mediators.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman develops a diffuse maculopapular rash, profuse diarrhea, and rising bilirubin 4 weeks after an allogeneic bone marrow transplant. Skin biopsy shows patchy epithelial cell death, yet the pathologist notes that the tissue is not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes. Which of the following best explains the severity of tissue injury despite the sparse infiltrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complement fixation by pre-formed recipient antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytokine release in addition to direct CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgE-triggered mast cell degranulation within the dermis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune-complex deposition along the dermal-epidermal junction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation in dermal arterioles

explanation.summary: GVHD injury is believed to result from cytokine release plus direct CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity, so tissues need not be heavily infiltrated.
explanation.whyCorrect: In GVHD, although tissue injury can be severe, affected tissues are not usually heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes. It is believed that damage is caused by cytokine release in addition to direct cytotoxicity by donor CD8+ T cells, consistent with the type IV (T-cell mediated) nature of GVHD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pre-formed recipient antibodies activating complement cause hyperacute rejection of a solid organ, not GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is type I hypersensitivity and does not explain T-cell-driven epithelial cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune-complex deposition is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism, not the cell-mediated injury of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation is the vascular lesion of chronic rejection (graft arteriosclerosis), not GVHD skin injury.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a rising serum creatinine 3 weeks after kidney transplantation. Biopsy shows interstitial inflammatory cells infiltrating between tubular epithelial cells. The graft is still well perfused. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanation.summary: Acute rejection is the principal cause of early graft failure and responds to immunosuppressive medication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tubulitis 3 weeks after transplant is acute cellular rejection. Acute rejection occurs 1 week to several months after transplant, is the principal cause of early graft failure, and responds to immunosuppressive medication, so the appropriate step is to treat with intensified immunosuppression rather than abandon the graft.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Withdrawing immunosuppression would allow the T-cell attack on the graft to accelerate and hasten graft failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Untreated acute rejection is the principal cause of early graft failure; observation alone risks losing the graft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immediate graft removal is the management of hyperacute rejection, in which the graft is thrombosed and necrotic; acute rejection is treatable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The biopsy shows rejection, not infection; antibiotics do not treat T-cell mediated tubulitis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has worsening graft function 5 weeks after kidney transplantation. Biopsy shows an arteriole in which inflammatory cells are attacking and undermining the endothelium (endothelitis), together with interstitial inflammation. Immunoperoxidase staining for C4d in peritubular capillaries is negative. Which of the following best describes the process?

explanation.summary: Rejection vasculitis (endothelitis) with a negative C4d stain is acute cellular (T-cell mediated) rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute cellular rejection is mediated by CD8+ T cells directly destroying graft cells and CD4+ T cells secreting cytokines that induce inflammation. In a kidney graft it manifests as tubulitis and as rejection vasculitis, in which inflammatory cells attack and undermine the endothelium of an arteriole (endothelitis). The absence of C4d deposition argues against an antibody-mediated process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute antibody-mediated rejection is marked by capillaritis with C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries; the negative C4d stain excludes it here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic rejection develops months to years later with intimal smooth muscle proliferation, interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GVHD involves donor T cells attacking recipient tissue after bone marrow transplant and does not cause vasculitis of a kidney graft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours and shows platelet-fibrin thrombi and ischemic necrosis, not T-cell endothelitis weeks later.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A pathologist examines a kidney graft biopsy showing acute cellular rejection. In addition to CD8+ T cells directly killing parenchymal cells, alloantigen-specific CD4+ T cells are contributing to interstitial inflammation. Which of the following cells are recruited to the graft by the cytokines these CD4+ T cells secrete?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts

explanation.summary: In acute cellular rejection, CD4+ T-cell cytokines recruit macrophages and neutrophils that cause interstitial inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute T-cell mediated rejection involves direct killing of graft cells by CD8+ T cells and inflammation caused by cytokines produced by CD4+ T cells. Those cytokines recruit macrophages and neutrophils, which together with parenchymal cell damage produce the interstitial inflammation seen on biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Natural killer cells and eosinophils are not described as the recruited inflammatory cells in acute cellular rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma cells and mast cells are not the effector cells recruited by CD4+ T-cell cytokines in acute cellular rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelets contribute to the fibrin-platelet thrombi of hyperacute rejection, not to T-cell mediated interstitial inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vascular smooth muscle proliferation is the intimal lesion of chronic rejection, not an acute recruited inflammatory infiltrate.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is preparing to be discharged after an uncomplicated kidney transplant. She is currently taking five immunosuppressive drugs and asks how long she will need medication to prevent rejection. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single drug is sufficient after the first month

choices.label: B
choices.text: All immunosuppressive drugs can be stopped once the graft is functioning at 1 year

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drugs are required only if a rejection episode occurs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four or more drugs must be continued for life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most recipients need two to three drugs throughout their lifespan

explanation.summary: Transplant recipients typically take four or more drugs early on and two to three drugs lifelong to prevent rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: It is common for transplant recipients to be taking four or more immunosuppressive drugs in the days immediately after surgery. Most recipients then require two to three drugs throughout their lifespan to prevent rejection, including chronic rejection, which immunosuppressive drugs act to prevent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick states most recipients require two to three drugs, not one, for life.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppression is not stopped after a year; chronic rejection can occur months to years later and is prevented by ongoing drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunosuppressive drugs are given continuously to prevent rejection, not only reactively after rejection begins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Four or more drugs are typical only in the days immediately after surgery, not lifelong.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 8 months ago presents with fever, cough, and a new pulmonary infiltrate. He is taking three immunosuppressive drugs and has had no rejection episodes. Which of the following best explains his susceptibility to this illness?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor T cells attacking his respiratory epithelium

explanation.summary: Immunosuppressive drugs prevent rejection but place transplant recipients at risk for infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most transplant recipients require two to three immunosuppressive drugs throughout their lifespan to prevent rejection. These drugs suppress the immune system, so patients are at risk for infections, which explains his pneumonia in the absence of any rejection episode.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pre-formed antibodies activating complement cause hyperacute rejection of the graft within 24 hours, not a lung infection months later.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue is GVHD, which is characteristic of bone marrow, not kidney, transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Graft arteriosclerosis of chronic rejection affects the transplanted organ's vessels, not the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune-complex deposition is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism and does not explain infectious susceptibility.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant 6 years ago has slowly rising creatinine and proteinuria. Biopsy shows inflammatory cells within glomerular capillary loops, accumulation of mesangial matrix, and duplication of the glomerular capillary basement membrane, along with interstitial fibrosis. Which of the following best describes this process?

explanation.summary: Glomerulitis with mesangial matrix accumulation, basement membrane duplication, and interstitial fibrosis years after transplant is chronic rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rejection occurs months to years after transplant and involves both cellular and humoral immune responses. In a kidney graft it produces glomerulitis, with inflammatory cells within the capillary loops, accumulation of mesangial matrix, and duplication of the capillary basement membrane, plus interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, in addition to graft arteriosclerosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute antibody-mediated rejection presents within weeks to months with peritubular capillaritis and C4d deposition, not years-long glomerular remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute cellular rejection occurs 1 week to several months after transplant and shows tubulitis and endothelitis, not basement membrane duplication and fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GVHD is a complication of bone marrow transplant in which donor T cells attack recipient organs, not a lesion of a kidney graft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperacute rejection occurs within 24 hours with platelet-fibrin thrombi and ischemic necrosis of the glomerulus.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man with a kidney transplant performed 5 years ago undergoes biopsy for progressive graft dysfunction. A trichrome-stained section shows large blue-staining areas surrounding shrunken tubules, contrasting with adjacent normal-appearing parenchyma. Which of the following do the blue areas represent?

explanation.summary: In chronic rejection, trichrome stain highlights interstitial fibrosis (blue) accompanying tubular atrophy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rejection, occurring months to years after transplant, produces interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. On a trichrome stain the blue area shows fibrosis, contrasted with the normal kidney, and the shrunken tubules within it represent tubular atrophy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C4d deposition is demonstrated by immunoperoxidase staining of peritubular capillaries in acute antibody-mediated rejection, not by trichrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tubulitis is an inflammatory cell infiltrate between tubular epithelial cells in acute cellular rejection, not a blue collagen-rich area.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesangial matrix accumulation is a glomerular feature of chronic rejection, not the interstitial blue-staining region around tubules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet-fibrin thrombi are the glomerular lesion of hyperacute rejection within 24 hours, not a years-later interstitial change.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 58-year-old heart transplant recipient develops diffuse concentric narrowing of the coronary arteries 3 years after transplantation. Histology shows chronic inflammation in the vessel wall with intimal smooth muscle proliferation and vessel occlusion. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this vascular lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes lodging within the coronary vessel wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytokines from alloreactive T cells and antibody binding to endothelial antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor-derived T cells recognizing the recipient's vascular tissue as foreign

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and histamine release in the adventitia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pre-formed recipient IgM antibodies triggering intravascular thrombosis

explanation.summary: Graft arteriosclerosis in chronic rejection is driven by T-cell cytokines together with antibody deposition on the endothelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rejection involves both cellular and humoral immune responses. Graft arteriosclerosis is caused by cytokines from alloantigen-specific CD4+ T cells and antibody binding to endothelial antigens, producing a chronic inflammatory reaction in the vessel wall, intimal smooth muscle proliferation, and vessel occlusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune-complex deposition is a type III mechanism; chronic rejection involves direct antibody binding to endothelial antigens plus T-cell cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue is the mechanism of GVHD after bone marrow transplant, not chronic rejection of a solid organ.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE and mast cells mediate type I hypersensitivity and play no role in graft arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pre-formed antibodies triggering thrombosis cause hyperacute rejection within minutes to 24 hours, not intimal proliferation years later.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man underwent heart transplantation 3 months ago. A surveillance endomyocardial biopsy is obtained to assess for rejection. Which of the following standardized histologic criteria are used to diagnose and grade rejection in this organ?

explanation.summary: ISHLT criteria grade rejection in heart transplants; Banff criteria are for kidney transplants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several histologic criteria have been created to diagnose and grade rejection for organ transplants. The ISHLT criteria are applied to heart transplants, whereas the Banff criteria are used for kidney transplants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Banff criteria grade rejection in kidney transplants, not heart transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duke criteria are used to diagnose infective endocarditis, not transplant rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Jones criteria are used to diagnose acute rheumatic fever, not graft rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Light's criteria distinguish transudative from exudative pleural effusions, not rejection grading.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to classify the forms of transplant rejection by whether antibodies contribute to graft injury. Which of the following is mediated by T cells without an antibody component?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rejection due to natural anti-ABO antibodies

explanation.summary: Acute cellular rejection is purely T-cell mediated; hyperacute, acute antibody-mediated, and chronic rejection all involve antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute cellular rejection occurs when CD8+ T cells directly destroy graft cells or CD4+ T cells secrete cytokines and induce inflammation; no antibody is involved. In contrast, hyperacute rejection is caused by pre-formed antibodies, acute antibody-mediated rejection by antibodies binding endothelium and activating complement, and chronic rejection involves both cellular and humoral responses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute antibody-mediated rejection is by definition antibody driven, with C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic rejection involves both cellular and humoral immune responses, with antibody deposition contributing to graft arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperacute rejection is caused by pre-formed recipient antibodies against ABO or class I MHC antigens activating complement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Natural IgM antibodies against blood group antigens mediate hyperacute rejection, an antibody-dependent process.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old kidney transplant recipient develops graft dysfunction 7 weeks after surgery. Biopsy shows inflammatory cells between tubular epithelial cells and, in a separate area, peritubular capillaritis with strong C4d deposition on immunoperoxidase staining. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute cellular and acute antibody-mediated rejection are both present

choices.label: B
choices.text: The C4d staining indicates hyperacute rejection superimposed on tubulitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The findings represent early chronic rejection with humoral features

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pattern indicates graft-versus-host disease of the transplanted kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tubulitis excludes an antibody-mediated process, so C4d is an artifact

explanation.summary: Acute rejection has two patterns, cellular and antibody-mediated, and most patterns may coexist in a given patient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute rejection occurs 1 week to several months after transplant via both cell-mediated (T-cell) and antibody-mediated (B-cell) mechanisms. It is divided into acute cellular rejection (tubulitis from T-cell attack) and acute antibody-mediated rejection (capillaritis with C4d deposition), but most patterns may be present in a given patient, so this biopsy shows both processes simultaneously.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours with thrombosis and necrosis, not at 7 weeks with capillaritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic rejection develops months to years later with graft arteriosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy, none of which are described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GVHD occurs when donor T cells attack the recipient after bone marrow transplant and is rare after solid organ transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two acute patterns are not mutually exclusive; C4d deposition is the diagnostic marker of antibody-mediated rejection, not an artifact.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia is scheduled for an allogeneic bone marrow transplant. He asks why he must receive chemotherapy before the healthy donor marrow is infused. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To deplete alloreactive T cells from the donor graft before it is infused

choices.label: B
choices.text: To eradicate his own marrow, removing cancerous cells and providing a clean slate

choices.label: C
choices.text: To induce tolerance in the donor T cells toward his own tissue antigens

choices.label: D
choices.text: To prevent graft arteriosclerosis from narrowing the marrow sinusoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: To remove pre-formed anti-donor antibodies capable of causing hyperacute rejection

explanation.summary: Recipient marrow is eradicated with chemotherapy to remove cancerous cells and provide a clean slate for the allogeneic graft.
explanation.whyCorrect: In an allogeneic bone marrow transplant, bone marrow cells from a non-identical donor are transplanted into a recipient whose bone marrow has been eradicated with chemotherapy to remove cancerous cells and provide a clean slate for the transplant. As the case discussion notes, it is important to wipe out the cancer cells from the patient's marrow before giving the donor's healthy marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemotherapy is given to the recipient to eradicate his marrow; it is not a method of removing T cells from the donor graft.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chemotherapy does not induce tolerance in donor T cells; GVHD risk is mitigated afterward with immunosuppressive drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Graft arteriosclerosis is a lesion of chronic solid organ rejection and is unrelated to pre-transplant conditioning.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperacute rejection from pre-formed antibodies is a solid organ phenomenon; conditioning chemotherapy is aimed at the recipient's marrow, not antibodies.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with leukemia is preparing for an allogeneic bone marrow transplant. Several relatives are being evaluated as potential donors. Independent of HLA matching, which of the following donor-recipient combinations is a recognized contributing factor for graft-versus-host disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor of the same ABO blood group as the recipient

explanation.summary: Transplantation from a female donor to a male recipient is a contributing factor for GVHD.
explanation.whyCorrect: GVHD occurs most frequently in recipients who have been exposed to radiation or who have leukemia, autoimmune diseases, or immunodeficiencies. Other contributing factors include transplantation from female donors to male recipients, making this pairing the recognized risk among those listed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABO compatibility relates to hyperacute rejection of solid organs; it is not described as a GVHD risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Donor age relative to the recipient is not listed as a contributing factor for GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick identifies female donor to male recipient, not male donor to female recipient, as the contributing factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Male-to-male transplantation is not the sex-mismatch pairing identified as a contributing factor for GVHD.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with a congenital immunodeficiency receives an allogeneic bone marrow transplant and develops severe graft-versus-host disease. His physician explains that his underlying immunodeficiency increased his risk. Which of the following best explains this relationship?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His deficient immune system overproduced pre-formed anti-donor antibodies against the graft

choices.label: B
choices.text: His immunodeficiency caused the donor marrow to undergo hyperacute rejection within hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunodeficiency increased the number of mature T lymphocytes contained in the infused donor marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunodeficiency promoted immune-complex deposition in the vessels of his skin and gut

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immunosuppression of the recipient reduced his ability to neutralize the donor T-lymphocyte attack

explanation.summary: Immunosuppressed recipients are less able to neutralize the attack by donor T lymphocytes, increasing GVHD risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: GVHD occurs most frequently in recipients exposed to radiation or with leukemia, autoimmune diseases, or immunodeficiencies. Some of these risk factors may be due to immunosuppression of the recipient, leading to a decrease in the ability of the recipient to neutralize the T-lymphocyte attack from the donor, so the donor T cells attack his organs unopposed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GVHD is mediated by donor T cells, not recipient antibodies, and an immunodeficient recipient would not overproduce antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperacute rejection is a recipient antibody attack on a solid organ graft; GVHD is the reverse direction and involves donor T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The T-cell content of the donor marrow is a property of the graft and is not altered by the recipient's immune status.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune-complex deposition is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism; GVHD is a type IV, T-cell mediated reaction.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is 3 weeks post allogeneic bone marrow transplant. She develops a maculopapular rash, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain with diarrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly with rising bilirubin. Which of the following sets of organs is characteristically involved when GVHD symptoms appear within weeks of transplant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow, thymus, and cervical lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brain, peripheral nerves, and skeletal muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heart, lung parenchyma, and both kidneys

choices.label: D
choices.text: Joints, eyes, and the pancreatic islets

explanation.summary: Early GVHD characteristically targets the skin, liver, and gastrointestinal tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with GVHD may present with a maculopapular rash, jaundice from destruction of small bile ducts, nausea, diarrhea from mucosal ulceration of the gut, vomiting, abdominal pain, and hepatosplenomegaly. Symptoms may appear within weeks after transplant, especially involving the skin, liver, and gastrointestinal tract, or later, up to several years after transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GVHD is an attack on the recipient's organs by donor T cells; lymphoid organs are not the characteristic early targets described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuromuscular tissues are not the described sites of early GVHD injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heart, lungs, and kidneys are not the organs the brick identifies as targets of early GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Joints, eyes, and pancreas are not the characteristic early targets; the pancreas is mentioned only as the target in type I diabetes, a type IV example.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man who received an allogeneic bone marrow transplant 3 years ago develops tight, thickened skin over his forearms. Biopsy shows a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction, a thinned epidermis, and thickened collagen bundles in the dermis. Which of the following best describes these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute graft-versus-host disease with epidermal apoptosis and dermal lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease with epidermal atrophy and dermal sclerosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic rejection with intimal smooth muscle proliferation and vessel occlusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type I hypersensitivity with mast cell mediator release and dermal edema

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type III hypersensitivity with immune-complex deposition and dermal vasculitis

explanation.summary: Chronic GVHD of the skin shows a sparse junctional lymphocytic infiltrate, thinned epidermis (atrophy), and thickened dermal collagen (sclerosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: GVHD symptoms can appear later, up to several years after transplant. In chronic GVHD of the skin there is a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction, the epidermis is thinned, signifying atrophy, and the underlying dermis shows thickening of collagen bundles, indicative of sclerosis, which explains the tight, thickened skin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute GVHD shows patchy epithelial cell death with dermal infiltrates of lymphocytes and macrophages, appearing within weeks, not epidermal atrophy with sclerosis years later.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation is graft arteriosclerosis in chronic rejection of a solid organ, not a skin lesion after marrow transplant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type I hypersensitivity produces vasodilation, edema, and smooth muscle contraction from mast cell mediators, not collagen thickening.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune-complex deposition is a type III mechanism; GVHD is a type IV, T-cell mediated process without immune-complex vasculitis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman develops a maculopapular rash, watery diarrhea, and jaundice 5 weeks after an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for leukemia. A diagnosis of graft-versus-host disease is made. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgical removal of the transplanted tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion of additional donor T cells

explanation.summary: Immunosuppressive drugs are used both to prevent and to treat GVHD.
explanation.whyCorrect: GVHD results from donor T cells attacking the recipient's organs, producing rash, diarrhea, and jaundice. Immunosuppressive drugs are used to both prevent and treat GVHD, as the case discussion emphasizes that medications to suppress the immune system help mitigate this risk after bone marrow transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics address the infection risk of immunosuppressed patients but do not treat the T-cell mediated organ injury of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conditioning chemotherapy is given before transplant to eradicate the recipient's marrow; it is not a treatment for established GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removing the graft is the management of a hyperacutely rejected solid organ; transplanted marrow cannot be surgically removed, and the patient depends on it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Donor T cells are the cells causing GVHD; infusing more would worsen the attack on her tissues.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has a 2-year history of crampy abdominal pain, diarrhea, and a 7-kg weight loss. Endoscopy with biopsies is performed. The duodenal mucosa shows a villous height-to-crypt ratio of 3:1. A sigmoid colon biopsy shows neutrophils packed within colonic crypts and a nodular aggregate of histiocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A nodular aggregate of histiocytes is a non-caseating granuloma, the histologic hallmark of Crohn disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-caseating granulomas, seen as nodular aggregates of histiocytes, are the histologic hallmark of Crohn disease. Active disease also shows acute and chronic inflammation with crypt abscesses, which are aggregates of neutrophils within the tube-like colonic glands, and distortion of the crypts. The duodenal villous height-to-crypt ratio of 3:1 is normal, so a small-bowel enteropathy does not explain the picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni causes invasive, often bloody diarrhea with fever, but it does not feature granulomatous inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Celiac disease produces marked villous atrophy and flattening; a villous height-to-crypt ratio of 3:1 is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clostridium difficile toxins damage the mucosa and produce pseudomembranes rather than granulomatous inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulcerative colitis also produces crypt abscesses, ulceration, and architectural distortion, but it characteristically lacks granulomas.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 6 months of diarrhea, bloating, and fatigue that worsen after meals containing wheat. Duodenal biopsy shows blunted villi with a dense intraepithelial CD8+ T-cell infiltrate and enterocyte damage. Gliadin is thought to trigger release of a cytokine that stimulates these CD8+ T cells. Which cytokine is responsible for that early step?

explanation.summary: In celiac disease, gliadin triggers IL-15 release, which stimulates CD8+ T cells and injures enterocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gliadin, a constituent of the grain protein gluten, can trigger release of IL-15 in susceptible patients. IL-15 stimulates CD8+ T cells, and the resulting inflammation damages enterocytes. That damage allows more gliadin to reach the lamina propria, where gliadin-derived peptides engage HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 class II molecules and recruit CD4+ T cells for further injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Interferon-gamma activates macrophages, but the gliadin-triggered cytokine that stimulates CD8+ T cells in this enteropathy is IL-15.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine and would not drive the CD8+ T-cell activation that injures enterocytes here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interleukin-4 drives B-cell responses and class switching; it is not the cytokine released by gliadin to stimulate CD8+ T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha is a general mediator of inflammation, not the specific gliadin-triggered stimulus for CD8+ T cells.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea and iron deficiency. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy, and her symptoms and histology resolve on a gluten-free diet. Her younger brother is now being evaluated, and HLA typing is ordered. Which pair of alleles is most strongly associated with her condition?

explanation.summary: Celiac disease is associated with the MHC class II alleles HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once gliadin reaches the lamina propria, gliadin-derived peptides are presented by HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 MHC class II molecules. That presentation stimulates CD4+ T cells, generating the additional inflammation and tissue damage that produce villous atrophy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-DR2 is associated with Goodpasture syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus rather than gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither allele is among the class II molecules that present gliadin peptides to CD4+ T cells in this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and has no role in presenting gliadin peptides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-B27 is the allele linked to reactive arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with biopsy-proven celiac disease develops intensely itchy, grouped blisters over both elbows, the upper back, and the buttocks. Skin biopsy shows separation of the epithelium from the basement membrane. The IgA antibodies responsible are directed against dietary gluten but cross-react with a connective tissue protein that anchors the epidermal basement membrane. Which protein is that target?

explanation.summary: Dermatitis herpetiformis results from IgA antibodies to gluten that cross-react with reticulin in the skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: In dermatitis herpetiformis, patients develop IgA antibodies to dietary gluten that cross-react with reticulin, a connective tissue protein important in anchoring the epidermal basement membrane. The IgA-mediated damage produces subepidermal blisters, classically on extensor surfaces as well as the upper back and buttocks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desmoglein 3 is an intercellular desmosomal protein, not the basement membrane anchoring protein targeted in this celiac-associated blistering disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Laminin 332 resides in the lamina lucida and is not the cross-reactive target of the gluten-directed IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plectin is a hemidesmosomal linker protein and is unrelated to the IgA cross-reactivity described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type VII collagen forms anchoring fibrils but is not the reticulin target implicated in dermatitis herpetiformis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and duodenal villous flattening develops grouped erythematous vesicles over the extensor surfaces of both elbows. Perilesional skin is submitted for direct immunofluorescence. Which finding is most expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granular IgA at the tips of the dermal papillae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granular IgM around the follicular openings

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intercellular IgG in a net-like epidermal pattern

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linear IgA along the epidermal basement membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linear IgG along the dermoepidermal junction

explanation.summary: Dermatitis herpetiformis shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an IgA-mediated condition associated with celiac disease. Microscopically there is separation of the epithelium from the basement membrane, producing a subepidermal blister, and immunofluorescence demonstrates granular IgA deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granular IgM at follicular openings is not the described finding; the immunoglobulin class in this disease is IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An intercellular net-like pattern reflects antibodies against desmosomal proteins, not the papillary-tip deposits seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The deposits in dermatitis herpetiformis are granular and confined to the papillary tips rather than a continuous linear band.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A linear IgG band is not the pattern of this IgA-mediated disease, in which the deposits are granular and of IgA class.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea, fatigue, and weight loss, and groups of erythematous blisters over both elbows. Duodenal biopsy shows flattening of the villi with loss of the normal finger-like projections. Which of the following is the cornerstone of her management?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surgical resection of the affected bowel

explanation.summary: Avoidance of gluten is the mainstay of treatment for celiac disease and its associated dermatitis herpetiformis.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has celiac disease, in which an immune response to gliadin produces duodenal villous atrophy and malabsorption, with dermatitis herpetiformis as a blistering extraintestinal manifestation. Because gliadin is the trigger, avoidance of dietary gluten is the cornerstone of treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactose is not the trigger in this disease; the inflammation is driven by gliadin, a constituent of the grain protein gluten.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metronidazole targets infectious causes of diarrhea and does nothing for an immune response directed against a dietary protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Systemic steroids are not the mainstay here, because withdrawing the inciting dietary antigen reverses the enteropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resection is not indicated, since the villous atrophy is an immune response to a dietary antigen rather than a focal lesion.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has several months of diarrhea, bloating, and fatigue. Serologic evaluation supports gluten-sensitive enteropathy, and duodenal biopsies are obtained. Which histologic finding is most expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Non-caseating granulomas in the lamina propria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Villous atrophy with flattening of the mucosa

explanation.summary: Celiac disease produces marked duodenal villous atrophy in place of the normal villous height-to-crypt ratio of at least 3:1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adult patients with celiac disease present with diarrhea, bloating, and fatigue. The ongoing gliadin-driven inflammation destroys enterocytes, and the normal finger-like duodenal villi are replaced by a flattened mucosa. Instead of a normal villous height-to-crypt ratio of at least 3:1, marked villous atrophy is seen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nodular histiocyte aggregates are the hallmark of Crohn disease and are not part of the celiac disease biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Large intranuclear inclusions indicate cytomegalovirus infection, typically in immunosuppressed patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adherent fibrinopurulent membranes reflect toxin-mediated injury from Clostridium difficile rather than gluten sensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inflammation through the full thickness of the bowel wall is a feature of Crohn disease, not of a gliadin-driven enteropathy.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is diagnosed with Crohn disease after presenting with chronic diarrhea, right lower quadrant pain, and weight loss. Although this disorder can involve any portion of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus, which region is most commonly affected?

explanation.summary: Crohn disease can involve any part of the gut but most commonly affects the terminal ileum, ileocecal valve, and cecum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crohn disease may affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract, including the mouth and anus, but it most commonly involves the terminal ileum, the ileocecal valve, and the cecum. This distribution explains the right lower quadrant pain and is one of the features that distinguishes it from ulcerative colitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Esophageal and cardia involvement is possible given the full gastrointestinal range of the disease but is not the usual site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastroduodenal involvement can occur in Crohn disease but is far less common than ileocecal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proximal small-bowel disease occurs but is not the classic distribution that defines this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rectal and distal colonic disease with continuous proximal extension is the pattern of ulcerative colitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with Crohn disease develops feculent drainage from a perianal opening and, several months later, obstructive symptoms from a narrowed segment of terminal ileum. At operation, the serosa of the involved bowel is erythematous. Which feature of his disease best explains these complications?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continuous involvement of the colonic mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inflammation spanning the full thickness of the wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Superficial ulceration limited to the mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Villous atrophy from an immune response to gliadin

explanation.summary: Transmural inflammation in Crohn disease produces strictures, fistula tracts, perforations, and serositis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inflammation of Crohn disease is transmural, meaning it involves the entire thickness of the bowel wall. As a result, patients may develop strictures, which are areas of pathologic narrowing, fistula tracts, which are abnormal connections between organs, and even perforations. Because the process reaches the serosa, erythematous serositis is seen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuous mucosal involvement describes ulcerative colitis, which does not typically produce fistulas or strictures.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disease confined to the mucosa and superficial submucosa is the pattern of ulcerative colitis and spares the deeper wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxin-mediated surface injury produces pseudomembranes, not the deep tracts and fibrotic narrowing described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An immune response to gliadin flattens duodenal villi and causes malabsorption rather than fistulas and strictures.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A colectomy specimen from a 38-year-old woman shows red, granular mucosa extending continuously from the rectum to the splenic flexure, with inflammatory pseudopolyps and a sharp demarcation from uninvolved mucosa. Histology shows crypt abscesses and inflammation limited to the mucosa and superficial submucosa. Which additional gross finding is most expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fibrotic stricture of the terminal ileum

explanation.summary: Because ulcerative colitis spares the deeper wall, the serosal surface appears normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ulcerative colitis the inflammation is limited to the mucosa and superficial submucosa rather than being transmural. As a consequence, strictures, perforations, and fistulas would be unusual, and the serosal surface appears normal, in direct contrast to Crohn disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This disorder is limited to the colon and rectum, and fibrotic narrowing of the ileum is not part of its picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serosal inflammation indicates that disease has reached the outer wall, which is characteristic of Crohn disease instead.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perforation follows transmural injury and would be unusual in a process confined to the mucosa and superficial submucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abnormal connections between bowel loops require inflammation through the full wall thickness, which this disease lacks.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A resected ileal segment from a 33-year-old man with Crohn disease has a gross mucosal surface that resembles cobblestones. Which of the following best explains this appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circumferential fibrous scars contracting the bowel into rings

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continuous mucosal inflammation extending from the rectum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diseased mucosa separated by intervening uninvolved mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regenerating islands of mucosa left by confluent ulceration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Submucosal lymphoid follicles enlarged by chronic antigen load

explanation.summary: The cobblestone appearance of Crohn disease comes from diseased mucosa alternating with intervening uninvolved mucosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crohn disease classically presents as skip lesions, areas of disease separated by uninvolved mucosa. Grossly this produces a surface resembling cobblestones, because diseased mucosa is interrupted by intervening non-involved mucosa. Aphthous ulcers in the bowel may also coalesce into linear, rake-like ulcers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrous narrowing produces a stricture, a separate complication of transmural inflammation, rather than a cobblestone surface.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuous inflammation spreading proximally from the rectum characterizes ulcerative colitis, which does not cobblestone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Islands of regenerating mucosa describe inflammatory pseudopolyps, a non-specific finding seen in both forms of the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enlarged submucosal lymphoid aggregates are not the basis of the cobblestone pattern described in this disease.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A colonic biopsy from a 30-year-old patient with active inflammatory bowel disease shows aggregates of neutrophils filling the tube-like glands of the colon, with distortion of those glands. What is this finding called?

explanation.summary: A crypt abscess is an aggregate of neutrophils within a colonic crypt, a marker of active inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crypt abscesses are aggregates of neutrophils within colonic crypts, the tube-like glands of the colon, and they mark active disease. As a result of the inflammation the crypts also become distorted. Crypt abscesses are seen in both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An aphthous ulcer is a shallow surface ulceration of mucosa, seen in the mouth and the bowel in Crohn disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A pseudopolyp is a gross projection of inflamed or regenerating mucosa rather than a collection of neutrophils in a gland.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A nodular aggregate of histiocytes, not neutrophils within glands, defines the granuloma characteristic of Crohn disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An owl's eye inclusion is a large intranuclear viral inclusion of cytomegalovirus infection, not a neutrophil aggregate.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: Two patients with chronic diarrhea undergo colonoscopy with biopsy: one is ultimately diagnosed with Crohn disease and the other with ulcerative colitis. Which of the following findings would be expected in both patients?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fistula tracts between adjacent bowel loops

choices.label: C
choices.text: Involvement of the terminal ileum and cecum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-caseating granulomas within the bowel wall

explanation.summary: Crypt abscesses, mucosal ulceration, pseudopolyps, and crypt distortion are common to both forms of inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease show acute and chronic inflammation, crypt abscesses, mucosal ulcerations, inflammatory pseudopolyps, and colonic architectural distortion. The key differences lie elsewhere: granulomas and transmural inflammation belong to Crohn disease, while ulcerative colitis is continuous and superficial.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Abnormal connections between organs follow transmural inflammation and would be unusual in ulcerative colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and rectum, so ileocecal involvement is not shared between the two disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomas are the histologic hallmark of Crohn disease, and their absence is a key feature of ulcerative colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inflammation through the full bowel wall is a defining feature of Crohn disease and does not occur in ulcerative colitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea
